Archaeologists conducting excavations along a new railway line in eastern England have discovered a rare coin from 287AD depicting the Roman usurper Carausius.

Excavations are ongoing at 1,000 trial trenches in Bedfordshire and Cambridgeshire along a planned East West railway line connecting Oxford, Bedford and Cambridge. Researchers are looking to build a detailed record of what lies underneath and help preserve archaeological heritage wherever possible.

They have already unearthed several ancient artefacts, including Roman coins and pottery and a Late Iron Age jar.

open image in gallery Roman coin from 287AD with an image of Carausius ( East West Rail )

Among the latest discoveries is a coin from 1,740 years ago bearing the name “Emperor Carausius”.

Carausius commanded a Roman fleet in the English Channel called “Classis Britannica”. He escaped to Britain and established an independent state after he was accused of embezzling captured pirate loot and Emperor Maximian ordered his execution.

The usurper declared himself Emperor of Britain and northern Gaul, establishing an independent state which he ruled from 286AD to 293AD. He was eventually murdered by his own finance minister, Allectus.

open image in gallery Trench digging for archaeological excavations ( East West Rail )

“Every discovery helps build a richer picture of the people who once lived here,” said archaeology survey manager Joss Piper-Jarrett.

“When you're excavating these features, you're often the first person to see them in 2,000 years, sometimes even longer, which is a really special feeling. It’s pretty amazing.”

Another Roman coin discovered during the excavations was dated to the 2nd century. It was likely minted under Emperor Antoninus Pius or Marcus Aurelius.

Archaeologists also unearthed a handmade rilled jar made of a fine shell and grog-tempered fabric dating to between 50BC and 50AD in the Late Iron Age.

open image in gallery Roman vase ( East West Rail )

Archaeologists plan to conduct excavations at 6,000 sites along the East West Rail route over a span of two years. “It's a really exciting time for the project because this programme represents an important step in helping us better understand the historic environment while continuing to progress East West Rail responsibly,” programme manager Jorn Pace said.

“By carrying out targeted investigations informed by detailed surveys, we can reduce unnecessary disturbance and ensure we take a careful approach to both the environment and the communities around us.”

After the excavations are over, the artefacts will be cleaned, analysed, recorded, and added to the archaeological archive.

The Independent is celebrating the biggest TV moments of the year so far, from the ones that got the nation talking to the scenes that moved us or made us laugh. In a series of articles running this summer, insiders share the part they played in making them happen.

He’s spent over half a century on our screens, and is one of the most revered broadcasters of his generation. As the face of Channel 4 News, where he worked for 32 years, he covered everything from the fall of the Berlin wall to Barack Obama’s inauguration. He interviewed Nelson Mandela straight out of prison, and faced down Margaret Thatcher no fewer than 20 times. So to see Jon Snow sitting in a doctor’s surgery, and struggling to remember the three words – “bus”, “door” and “rose” – that had been spoken to him mere moments earlier, came as a real shock.

The veteran journalist had invited the camera into that most intimate of settings for his film Jon Snow: A Last Big Story, a documentary that charted the devastating impact that Alzheimer’s is having on his brain. But he’s still got a nose for a story. While making the film, Snow stumbled on a scoop: the cover-up of a mining disaster that was destroying land and water in Zambia. Suddenly, the film became something else. It was not only a study of a man coping with a cruel condition, but a report on a scandal that made headlines around the world.

Director Laura Warner reflects on making a documentary that was sad, surprising, and beautiful, and reflected the complex journey Snow is now on.

What it was like to film the doctor’s surgery scene

“It was really difficult to film. It didn’t just land in our laps – it took literally months and months of conversations and negotiations with Jon, his wife Precious, and Jon’s doctors to arrange that scene. It was a genuine doctor’s appointment and Jon has them every six to 12 months. A lot can happen between the appointments so it is really exposing. Precious said, ‘OK, if I allow you to film it, then only you can be in the room and only you and the editor can look at the material. I’ll allow you to choose what will go into the film, and everything else will then be deleted and will never be seen again by anybody.’

Jon Snow in ‘A Last Big Story’ ( Channel 4 )

“It was very raw. All you see in the film is two or three minutes’ worth of material. But actually it was an hour-long appointment where you really understand the carnage that this disease can wreak on an individual, on their spouse, and on a person’s way of life and their future hopes and dreams.

“It was genuinely really upsetting, because by that point we’d been filming with Jon for a really long time and I knew and loved Jon and Precious a lot, and the realities of the disease are just really harsh. It was probably one of the hardest things I’ve ever filmed.

“There were a lot of other points during the filmmaking where I had to put the camera down and I thought, as a human being rather than a filmmaker: no, now’s the time to look after Jon. Now’s not the time to be filming.”

The doctors were on board straight away

“They understand the benefits of people opening up, because Alzheimer’s is really stigmatising, so people just feel that they want to hide their relatives and hide their loved ones, and they don’t want to expose them, because they feel that it’s embarrassing in some way. But one of the most important things that we all wanted to achieve with this documentary was to say, ‘You can come out, don’t feel stigmatised, don’t feel embarrassed,’ and to also to teach people who don’t have a relative with Alzheimer’s how to talk to people with the condition.”

The moving reaction to the documentary

“I don't think any of us expected it to have such an impact, but everybody has been reaching out to all of us and talking about their family members and the experiences they’ve had. They’ve talked about how they’re going to try and come out a little bit more into society and not be so embarrassed.

“We have a really long impact campaign that we’re working on with the Alzheimer’s Society, and we hope that the film won’t just instigate more work in terms of scientific developments, but it will actually help people come out from behind closed doors, because I think the stigma just kills you, you know? It really stops people with Alzheimer’s from interacting with society, and that really exacerbates the disease, and it does not help carers because they’re stuck behind closed doors just dealing with this, feeling like they’re alone.

“A lot of people who really care about Jon, for all the right reasons, were worried that the film would detract from Jon’s legacy as a war correspondent, a newscaster and a beloved national treasure. So I’m really pleased that actually, now, people have said that this is a really great secondary legacy to have. He has helped a lot of people understand that you should not feel stigmatised for having Alzheimer’s. Don’t hide. Come out.”

Most bus fares in England will be capped at £2 from January, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced.

Currently, the nationwide cap on single bus fares is set at £3 until the end of March 2027. However, some areas – including London and Greater Manchester, where Mr Burnham set a £2 limit as mayor – have lower top rates for single tickets.

“Good, affordable transport links are an essential. No one should be priced out of those and left behind,” Mr Burnham said.

“But for too long people have said that cheaper transport isn’t an option. I don’t accept that. I’ve done it before and I will do it again now: a £2 cap on bus fares for millions across the country.

“Lower fares will help people get to where they need to – giving them breathing space to help with the cost of living.”

The measure is backed by £454 million of funding – including money to allow devolved governments to take similar action.

open image in gallery Andy Burnham says: ’Good, affordable transport links are an essential’ ( PA )

Some £400 million of that funding will come from switching investment in international climate finance to loans, with the rest from savings in the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero budget. The total cost of the scheme is expected to be more than £500 million, with the rest coming from Department for Transport funding already allocated to buses.

The £2 cap will be in place throughout 2027 and reverses an increase put in place by Sir Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves in 2024.

A £2 cap had been in place between January 2023 and December 2024 but the incoming Labour administration argued it was not affordable, although some metro mayors, including Mr Burnham, decided to fund an extension of the lower limit in their areas.

Chancellor John Healey said “millions of people” would benefit from fares being slashed by a third and insisted the measure could be paid for.

“This action to ease the cost of living is funded by savings made elsewhere, so there’s no burden to British taxpayers, just pounds going back into their pockets,” he said.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said the move would make “everyday journeys easier and cheaper”.

open image in gallery Chancellor John Healey said ’millions of people’ would benefit from fares being slashed ( PA )

On Tuesday, Mr Burnham told ministers he will lead a “cost-of-living Government” after announcing an £850 million tax cut on electricity bills.

From October 1, electricity bills will be VAT-free, saving households about £45 a year as part of the new Prime Minister’s promise to help ease cost-of-living pressures.

But Darren Jones, a key ally of former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer who lost his Cabinet post on Monday when Mr Burnham took office, said the policy was “unfunded”.

Mr Burnham used the first meeting of his Cabinet to say that ministers must give people “a sense that help is coming”.

He vowed to always “show how we’re going to pay” for policies to help hard-pressed people.

Rebel Wilson has won a defamation case brought against her by actor Charlotte MacInnes, after an Australian judge dismissed claims that the Hollywood star’s Instagram posts about her The Deb co-star had harmed her reputation.

Justice Elizabeth Raper ruled on Wednesday that MacInnes had failed to establish the publications caused, or were likely to cause, serious harm, and ordered her to pay Wilson’s legal costs.

MacInnes, who played the lead role in Wilson’s directorial debut, The Deb, sued the Pitch Perfect and Bridesmaids actor over a series of Instagram posts published in 2024 and 2025.

She alleged the posts falsely suggested that she had withdrawn a complaint of sexual harassment against one of the film’s producers in order to advance her career, and argued that they exposed her to “abuse, hatred and ridicule online” while harming her employment prospects, according to court submissions.

Delivering her judgment, Justice Raper dismissed the case, concluding that MacInnes had “failed to establish that the publications have caused or were likely to cause serious harm”.

open image in gallery Charlotte MacInnes, who played the lead role in Wilson’s directorial debut, The Deb , sued the Pitch Perfect actor over a series of Instagram posts published in 2024 and 2025 ( Reuters )

During the trial, the judge said it was established that the only potentially defamatory meaning in Wilson’s posts was an allegation that MacInnes had changed her account of an incident involving one of the film’s producers, but ultimately ruled that this imputation was not defamatory.

The proceedings focused on a September 2023 incident that involved MacInnes and Amanda Ghost, one of The Deb’s producers. According to evidence heard by the court, Ghost suffered an adverse physical reaction after swimming at Sydney’s Bondi Beach.

The pair returned to a luxury apartment rented by the production, where Ghost showered while MacInnes prepared a bath. Both women told the court they entered the bath wearing swimsuits to warm up and insisted that “there was nothing sexual in any way”, with Ghost saying she had been shivering uncontrollably and had developed welts after the swim.

Justice Raper remarked during her ruling: “To say that the circumstances surrounding how they came to be in the bath are unusual would be an understatement.”

open image in gallery File: Rebel Wilson speaks to the media as she arrives at court on the first day of a nine-day defamation hearing in Sydney ( Reuters )

Wilson maintained throughout the proceedings that MacInnes had originally described the incident to her as making her feel “uncomfortable” after Ghost allegedly asked her to shower and bathe with her.

Wilson told the court she understood those remarks to amount to a report of sexual harassment and believed she had a responsibility as the film’s director to act upon them. She denied fabricating the allegations or raising them as leverage in separate disputes involving the film’s production.

During the hearing, Wilson said: “I am known as a truth-teller,” adding that her social media posts amounted to “telling the truth” rather than an attack on MacInnes.

MacInnes denied ever making or withdrawing a complaint of sexual harassment. During the trial, her barrister, Sue Chrysanthou SC, accused Wilson of carrying out a “complete revision of history” and described her as “a fantastical liar who has made up terrible, terrible allegations about multiple people”.

Wilson’s barrister, Dauid Sibtain SC, rejected those claims, arguing that his client “had no motive to lie” and contending that MacInnes had withdrawn the complaint because maintaining a positive relationship with Ghost would benefit her career.

Shortly after Wednesday’s ruling, Wilson posted on Instagram thanking Justice Raper and the Australian legal system for what she described as a “substantial win”.

The last time Mais al-Gharam saw her seven siblings was in the Gaza Strip two months before the war. That was before she left the Palestinian territory to go live in Israel and before an Israeli airstrike on the family's home killed her parents and younger brother.

But on this day, she waited hopefully outside Israel’s Kerem Shalom crossing, scanning for a glimpse of her surviving brothers and sisters as they made their way through the gates and out of Gaza.

“We never stopped being a family,” said Mais, who is 23 and the eldest of eight siblings born to a father from Gaza and a mother who was a Palestinian citizen of Israel. “But every day I wondered whether I’d see them again.”

The family finally reunited this month following a yearslong effort by Mais and a team of lawyers to get her brothers and sisters out. They met outside the border crossing and then drove together to the city of Nazareth, where their mother’s extended family showered the siblings with hugs and homemade food.

The reunion carried joy, grief and a quiet disbelief: Despite the odds, Mais had secured Israeli passports for her Gaza-born siblings, ages 8 to 22, and arranged for them to come live with her.

But while they had found one another again, they could never reclaim what they lost.

“It’s like coming back from the grave,” Faraj al-Gharam, their maternal grandfather, said of his grandchildren. In Gaza, he said, “human life has no value.”

Hundreds of Palestinian families are split between Israel and Gaza

The family’s story begins in 2002 when Murad al-Gharam, a native of Gaza, was working construction in Israel on a temporary job permit. There, he met and married Amal Karim, a Palestinian citizen of Israel who lived in Nazareth. Soon, they had a baby girl and named her Mais.

Decades ago, such marriages were common between Palestinians who lived in the West Bank, Gaza and Israel, before two Palestinian uprisings and Israel’s response closed off the occupied territories.

When Murad and Amal met, it was at the height of the Second Intifada. As violence raged, Israel clamped down on work permits for Palestinians, putting Murad’s status in Israel in jeopardy.

He and Amal moved to Gaza permanently, settling down with Mais in Nuseirat, a built-up refugee camp in the enclave’s central region. Murad began work as a taxi driver, and the couple had seven more children — Zuhour, 22; Jwaher, 21; Sabreen, 20; Ghfran, 17, Fady, 16; Maisara, 11; and Arjwan, 8.

“We lived here together as a family ... and never lacked anything,” Zuhour said.

On Oct. 7, 2023, everything changed.

When Hamas-led militants from Gaza attacked southern Israel, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 others hostage, the al-Gharams were one of what rights groups estimated to be more than 300 “divided families” with members on both sides of the border.

As Israel launched its retaliatory offensive, and prepared for a full-scale ground invasion, the family had to decide what to do.

Mais had already emigrated back to Nazareth, where she found a job and married. And while the seven children who were born in Gaza had the right to apply for Israeli citizenship through their mother, their father had no such option.

Israeli law generally bars the Palestinian spouses of Israeli citizens from obtaining permanent residency status. If the rest of the family wanted to leave, he would have to stay behind.

“We said, ‘Either we all leave together, or we all stay together,’” according to Zuhour.

So they braced for war.

A sister fears for her parents and siblings' survival

About 160 kilometers (100 miles) away, Mais waited anxiously each day for updates, which were infrequent after Israel cut off Gaza's electricity and took out cellphone and internet networks.

The al-Gharam family was displaced at least seven times in the first half of 2024, eventually landing in Rafah in southern Gaza, before Israel invaded there, too.

In the end, they returned to Nuseirat, about 10 kilometers (6 miles) south of Gaza City, and moved back into the home where the children grew up. The area was both a place of refuge and a site of regular airstrikes on schools and apartment buildings that Israel said were being used by Hamas.

At 6 a.m. on July 10, 2024, an airstrike tore into their home, collapsing walls and sending debris crashing through the ceiling. Dazed and wounded, the siblings ran into the street screaming for help.

Jwaher said she was in such shock that she couldn’t even feel that her leg and fingers had been fractured.

They piled into cars and rushed westward to Al Aqsa Hospital in the city of Deir al-Balah, where doctors treated them and pronounced their mother, father and brother Maisara dead.

“Suddenly the burden fell on us,” Sabreen said.

Together, they cooked, cleaned and collected firewood to boil water and keep warm. They also made money by opening a bakery in their neighborhood, while relying on charity and funds sent by relatives in Nazareth.

“We were forced — each of us — to take on a role that wasn’t ours,” Fady said.

The Israeli military did not respond to a request for comment on the strike.

Israeli lawyers pushed the government to reunite family

As her siblings kept the family afloat in Gaza, Mais sprang into action in Israel, determined to save them as conditions there rapidly deteriorated.

She contacted HaMoked, an Israeli rights group, on the day of the strike to start the paperwork and procedures required to reunite with her siblings and bring them to Nazareth. They began drafting letters to the Israeli Interior Ministry and COGAT, the military body that oversees crossings and humanitarian affairs in Gaza.

When she learned from her siblings that their parents and brother were dead, “it was the biggest shock I think I’ve ever gone through in my life,” she said.

At the time, reuniting seemed impossible. Mais needed permits for them to enter Israel, a court order appointing Zuhour, the eldest sibling in Gaza, as legal guardian to the minor children, and six successful applications for Israeli citizenship.

According to HaMoked, the Israeli Interior Ministry initially rejected the request to apply for the divided family procedure to reunite the al-Gharams because their mother was dead.

The family then had to undergo DNA testing to prove the siblings’ relationship to Mais, an Israeli citizen. Once the test results were in, the siblings had to make another trip to Kerem Shalom to sign the paperwork for their Israeli passports.

They finally arrived in Israel on July 8, nearly two years to the date of the deadly strike on their home.

The half-day journey to Nazareth took the siblings from Gaza’s rubble past Israel’s irrigated fields and modern cities. When they arrived, they spoke mostly about ordinary hopes such as spending time with relatives, going to school and seeing doctors. They said they had fulfilled their top priority: reuniting.

“Family,” Jwaher said, “is the most important thing.”

___

Mednick reported from Tel Aviv, Israel. Associated Press reporters Wafaa Shurafa in Deir al-Balah, Gaza Strip; Abdel Kareem Hana in Nuseirat, Gaza Strip; and Alon Bernstein and Mahmoud Illean in Nazareth, Israel, contributed to this report.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has apologised after comments he made about the early release of prisoners were inadvertently picked up by a microphone.

Mr Streeting made the remarks during a conversation with Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood and the new Justice Secretary Alex Norris on Tuesday.

In the overheard comments, Mr Streeting suggested to Ms Mahmood that Mr Norris was “the enemy now” and “wants to let them all out”. The exchange occurred on Tuesday, a day after Mr Streeting returned to Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s new-look Cabinet.

Taking to X, Mr Streeting clarified that his comment was a reference to a joke shared between former Conservative prime minister Theresa May and ex-chancellor and home secretary Kenneth Clarke.

He wrote: “I hope everyone can see there was no ill intent behind this ribbing of the new Justice Secretary – it was a reference to an old May/Clarke joke.

“But I appreciate these are very serious issues and am sorry for any offence inadvertently caused by this moment of levity.”

Ms Mahmood also said there was “no ill intent” about the “ribbing” of Mr Norris.

She wrote on X: “I appreciate this is an extremely serious issue and do not want anyone to mistake this moment of levity for a lack of serious intent.”

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch wrote on X: “While Andy Burnham’s cabinet are joking about letting criminals out of prison early, Conservatives are listening to victims and will continue to fight this disgusting policy.”

Under the new Sentencing Act, set to come into force in September, around 6,000 criminals are set to be released under the early prison release scheme.

Mr Norris has been urged to reconsider the early release scheme and when asked about reports that the Prime Minister could be working on exempting rapists and child groomers from the scheme, his spokesman said: “The Government’s fully focused on keeping the public safe.

“We’ve got no option but to take decisive action to fix the crisis in our prisons. I’m not going to get into speculation over possible policy changes.”

Mr Streeting’s comments come as the mother of police officer Andrew Harper said it feels like an “insult” that two of her son’s killers may be eligible for early release from prison.

Pc Harper was 28 when he sustained fatal injuries while responding to a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in August 2019.

Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were passengers in the car and both 17 years old at the time, were handed 13 years in custody for manslaughter after a trial at the Old Bailey in 2020.

Both men might be eligible to be released from prison halfway through their sentences, the Ministry of Justice has confirmed.

News.content:

Matt Damon revealed that some of the most talked-about shots of his muscular transformation in The Odyssey were made possible by a female stunt performer with “the greatest arms I’ve ever seen”.

Damon, 55, plays Odysseus in Christopher Nolan’s latest film, an adaptation of Homer’s Greek epic, which follows the hero’s long journey home to Ithaca after the Trojan War as he battles monsters, gods and mythical foes while his wife Penelope fends off suitors and his son Telemachus searches for him.

The ensemble cast also includes Anne Hathaway as Penelope, Tom Holland as Telemachus, Robert Pattinson as the suitor Antinous, Zendaya as Athena, Samantha Morton as Circe, Charlize Theron as Calypso, and Lupita Nyong'o as Helen of Troy. Jon Bernthal, Benny Safdie, John Leguizamo, Himesh Patel, Elliot Page, Bill Irwin, and Mia Goth feature as well.

Damon said his stunt double was used in scenes with the Laestrygonians, the race of giant cannibals from Homer’s Odyssey. The sequence required forced-perspective filmmaking, with unusually tall and unusually short stunt performers used to create the illusion of towering giants confronting Odysseus and his men.

“There were these stuntmen who were all seven feet and then they got stunt men who were under five feet,” Damon said on the Happy Sad Confused podcast.

“My double was a woman, a female stunt performer who had the greatest arms I’ve ever seen.”

Jimmy Gonzales as Cepheus, Matt Damon as Odysseus, and Himesh Patel as Eurylochus in The Odyssey ( Universal Pictures )

He said when he first met her in the catering tent during filming, he “went up and hugged her and thanked her for all the work she put in”.

“There are those shots where you see these giants looming over me,” he said. “It was almost 100 per cent my arms in the movie, but you got to give it up where it’s due.”

The stunt performer has since been identified as Devyn Dalton, who confirmed on social media that Damon was referring to her. Dalton, a Canadian stunt performer, has worked extensively across film and television. Her credits include The Last of Us, Percy Jackson and the Olympians, The Fall of the House of Usher, Thunderbolts, as well as Wonder, The BFG, Once Upon a Time, and X-Men: Dark Phoenix.

Dalton responded to Damon’s comments on her Instagram, writing: “This is wild and awesome. Appreciate all the support and shoutouts.”

She also shared photos from the sets of The Odyssey, describing her time shooting the battle sequence in the Scottish Highlands as “an adventure”.

“No spoilers just yet, but I’m incredibly grateful to be a part of the Laestrygonian battle. Stunt doubling the incredible Matt Damon. An epic team effort. We worked hard, shared plenty of laughs, and created memories I’ll never forget.”

Damon has previously talked about the physical training he underwent to take on the role after Nolan asked him to be “lean but strong”.

“I was in great shape. I lost a lot of weight,” the Good Will Hunting actor told Jason and Travis Kelce on their New Heights podcast in January.

Damon lost more than 20 pounds and underwent intense training to get in shape to play Odysseus. He said he weighed between 185 and 200 pounds before filming the movie, but worked with his doctor to cut gluten from his diet, which proved to be the key to his transformation.

“I did that whole movie at 167,” he said. “And I haven’t been that light since high school. So it was a lot of training and a really strict diet.”

In her five-star review of the new movie, The Independent’s Clarisse Loughrey described it as “Nolan’s best work to date”.

Nolan’s “stamp is all over the film – this is intellectual, brutalist, muscular Hollywood fare – yet it never wavers in its commitment to, and comprehension of, its source text,” she wrote. “There is not a single decision here that’s been thoughtlessly made, nor that I imagine Nolan himself couldn’t easily defend, much to the imagined chagrin of certain lawless parts of the internet.”

The Odyssey is enjoying a record-breaking theatrical debut with a $264.1m worldwide opening, including $124.5m in the US and Canada, making it the biggest global opening of Nolan’s career.

The Odyssey is screening in cinemas now.

News.title: Private sector pay suffers worst growth since Covid
News.content:
Private sector wages are growing at their slowest pace since the pandemic, piling pressure on Andy Burnham as he enters Downing Street facing a fragile economy and strained public finances.

Salaries rose by 2.9pc in the three months to May, the first time growth has dipped below 3pc since October 2020 and only narrowly ahead of inflation at 2.8pc.

The slowdown was most acute in key industries, with wages in finance and business services up just 2.3pc, manufacturing at 2.5pc and construction earnings falling by 0.2pc over the year.

In contrast, public sector pay accelerated to 5.5pc after striking workers secured higher settlements, widening the gap between state and private sectors.

The cooling labour market came as borrowing overshot official forecasts, leaving John Healey, the new Chancellor, with a £2.7bn gap against expectations.

The Government borrowed £57.6bn between April and June – less than a year earlier but still ahead of projections – pushing public debt to nearly £3tn, or 94.9pc of GDP.

Mr Healey said: “The Prime Minister and I have talked about how we will work in lockstep to meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty and how we’ll make life more affordable for working people right across the UK.”

However, Sir Mel Stride, the shadow business secretary, said: “If Andy Burnham and John Healey are really serious about the future of our economy then they must get borrowing under control.”

News.title: Scammers stole $114 billion as Southeast Asia’s crime gangs go corporate
News.content:
Scam gangs stole up to $114 billion from people in Asia-Pacific alone in 2025, the UN has warned, as crime syndicates rapidly professionalise their tactics to evade law enforcement in Southeast Asia.

By way of comparison, the sum dwarfs the $85 billion the UK spends each year on defence.

The Asia-Pacific region has emerged as an epicentre for massive cyber fraud operations since the Covid pandemic. Scammers – some willingly, others under duress – are now stealing billions from internet users across the world via fake romance and cryptocurrency investment schemes.

In 2025, these fraud operations stole between $88.3 and $114.1bn from just people across East Asia, Southeast Asia, Australia and New Zealand, according to a report on Tuesday from the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).

Those figures are triple the estimated losses in 2023, between $18 and $37bn, and don’t account for victims in Europe or the US.

The scam centres – which began in fortified compounds but are now increasingly housed in innocuous office blocks and villas – are found across the region, but have especially exploited power vacuums caused by war, corruption and weak governance in Cambodia, Myanmar and Laos.

Although the scammers initially targeted people in China, they have dramatically expanded their ambitions. The UNODC said people from at least 80 countries and territories had been identified in compounds, with recruiters seeking people from outside Asia as they look to expand new markets.

News.title: UK borrowing costs rise at fastest pace in G7
News.content:
Britain’s borrowing costs rose at the fastest pace in the G7 after Andy Burnham said he would take a “flexible” approach to the UK’s fiscal rules.

In his maiden speech as prime minister, Mr Burnham on Monday signalled he could bend the rules underpinning Britain’s finances, spooking financial markets fearful of higher government spending.

UK gilts – a benchmark for how much the Government pays on its debt – saw yields rise 0.08 percentage points to an eight-week high of 5.03pc for the 10-year bond. Thirty-year gilts also pushed higher.

The rise was the fastest in the G7, excluding Japan, whose markets are closed for a national holiday.

After markets closed on Monday, Mr Burnham surprised the City by picking John Healey as his next Chancellor.

Mr Healey, who quit over defence funding rising too slowly, will now be tasked with finding billions of pounds in Britain’s stretched public finances.

Shabana Mahmood, the Home Secretary, had widely been expected for the role. Ed Miliband, the former Energy Secretary, was also in contention.

Mr Healey will replace Rachel Reeves, who resigned on Monday.

The appointment of Mr Healey, a veteran of the Blair-Brown government, may calm fears in the City after Mr Burnham pledged to stretch the fiscal rules by using “flexibility” within them.

Speaking in Downing Street, Mr Burnham said: “I’ve said we’ll stick to the fiscal rules, and by that I mean the existing fiscal rules, and use obviously any flexibility within them.”

James Athey, a fund manager at Marlborough, said: “It’s not a good start because bandying around the words fiscal rules seems to be believed within government circles to be a sufficient condition to get financial markets on side, and that just misunderstands an element of the problem.”

He added that investors were watching closely for any signs that the Government will increase borrowing.

Matt Amis, investment director at Aberdeen, said Mr Burnham’s comments had “got the markets’ attention.”

He said “It just shows this week in particular the language from the Burnham administration, the new chancellor, is going to be key here. The gilt market is on edge.”

Mr Burnham, who has become the UK’s seventh prime minister in just a decade, has inherited a troubled economy as businesses grapple with low confidence and strained public finances.

Monday’s comment suggests the new prime minister will use measures to raise borrowing while keeping the additional sums off the Government’s book.

The Resolution Foundation, a think tank, said he could do this by expanding the remit of institutions like the National Wealth Fund, an arms-length government investment vehicle.

His plan to use “flexibility” in the fiscal rules comes after Ms Reeves altered the main indicator of government debt in 2024.

She tweaked the primary measure of the UK’s debt to Public Sector Net Financial Liabilities, meaning that when public financial institutions borrow to invest in a private business it does not count towards the government’s fiscal rules.

However, the think tank warned that boosting the financial capacity of public financial institutions like the National Wealth Fund by £16bn would cost around £400 million a year in debt interest.

Helen Miller, director at the Institute for Fiscal Studies, warned that challenging public finances will mean Mr Burnham will be forced to make tough choices on spending.

She said: “While chancellors come and go, the underlying fiscal constraints remain the same. Public debt, borrowing and debt-interest costs are all high. One in every £12 the government spends currently goes on debt interest.”

Higher borrowing costs threaten to increase the Government’s debt interest bill, which is already forecast to hit £111.2bn for the financial year - equivalent to 8.3pc of public spending.

Mr Burnham said he would announce a set of measures on Tuesday to give households “breathing space” to help with the cost of living.

“I will set out some of those measures starting tomorrow, including how we pay for them,” he said.

“We will help more young people into education... and we will build more council homes. That is the fair and sustainable way to bring the welfare bill down, to meet our fiscal rules and to honour our commitments on defence to our international partners.”

Mr Amis said: “Tomorrow we’re getting some cost of living news. [Burnham] said he was going to state where that funding’s come from. I think that’s key, any unfunded spending from here would get the market’s attention.”

News.title: India approves first dengue vaccine as cases surge in South Asia
News.content:
India has approved its first dengue vaccine as cases of the mosquito-borne disease surge in South Asia.

Japan’s Takeda Pharmaceutical’s dengue vaccine QDENGA has been approved by India’s drug regulator, the Centre Drugs Standard Control Organisation (CDSCO).

The global threat posed by dengue has been rising for years, as climate change, urbanisation and international travel aid the spread of the mosquitoes that transmit it.

The approval comes as hospitals across South Asia grapple with a surge in dengue infections.

In Sri Lanka, health authorities reported 2,652 new cases on Sunday alone, taking the total to 76,044 dengue cases so far this year. At least 53 people have died.

Bangladesh is also suffering a major outbreak with over 9,000 cases and 30 deaths that has piled pressure on its health system even as it battles a measles epidemic.

Dengue is transmitted to humans through the bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes.

Its symptoms include fever, severe muscle pain, and in severe cases, shock and internal bleeding that can be fatal.

Although mortality is relatively low, outbreaks place a substantial burden on health systems.

Takeda’s QDENGA jab is a live-attenuated tetravalent vaccine designed to protect against all four dengue virus serotypes. It can be given regardless of previous dengue infections.

“The approval comes at a critical time for public health, as reported dengue cases in India have increased 11-fold in the past two decades,” the company said in a statement.

News.title: Burnham’s plan to restore UK aid spending
News.content:
Andy Burnham is planning to reverse the cuts to Britain’s aid budget made by his predecessors Sir Keir Starmer and Rishi Sunak, according to reports.

A roadmap for returning the UK to spending 0.7 per cent of Gross National Income (GNI) on international aid will be drawn up as part of a major shake-up of the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office (FCDO), The Independent reported.

Ed Miliband is set to be named Foreign Secretary and put in charge of overhauling Britain’s international development aims, as well as prioritising climate goals, senior Labour sources said.

The aid spending plan was absent from Mr Burnham’s brief first speech as Prime Minister, in which he pledged to end rough sleeping and bring down the welfare bill in order to fund defence and council housing.

But it follows anger within the Labour Party over what was seen as a broken manifesto promise, when Sir Keir and Rachel Reeves, the Chancellor, slashed aid spending to 0.3 per cent of GNI.

Senior Labour MPs have been lobbying for a return to the 0.7 per cent commitment, a target first established by the United Nations in the 1970s.

It has since become a key yardstick for international efforts to reduce poverty and tackle major health issues like the HIV/AIDS epidemic, vaccine access, and maternal mortality in poor countries.

News.title: The best bars and nightlife in Lyon
News.content:
While drinking in this gourmet city remains firmly rooted in the surrounding Rhône Valley’s ancient wine-growing heritage, new-gen addresses have embraced world cocktail culture in style. They’re using Lyon’s long-envied gastronomic know-how and rich bounty of local seasonal produce to create some sensational new drinks and food pairings as only the French can. Artisanal spirits meanwhile are increasingly fashionable: cornichon gin, Mezcal-fuelled soirées at chef Carla Kirsch’s gourmet tacos joint in Croix-Rousse, and the stunning Christian Drouin gin and pine-needle liqueur cocktail with stick of Comté cheese to stir I recently had at Hôtel Dieu’s Le Dôme bar all spring to mind.

Come the warmer days of spring and summer, the city’s fervent café-life spills onto pretty pavement terraces, while floating bars moored along Les Berges du Rhône (the landscaped river banks of the Rhône’s Rive Gauche or Left Bank) hum with after-dark dance parties and festivities. Clubbing remains fairly mainstream.

Sports.title: Six standout World Cup stars who Man Utd could sign next for Michael Carrick rebuild
Sports.content:
Six standout World Cup stars who Man Utd could sign next for Michael Carrick rebuild

Manchester United could turn to some of the World Cup 2026's standout performers this summer as they continue adding to their ranks

View 2 Images Antonio Nusa is among the World Cup stars who Manchester United might look to pursue (Image: NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Manchester United have already been busy this summer, making multiple new signings as they look to give Michael Carrick plenty to work with ahead of a return to the Champions League. More are set to follow, with the World Cup putting plenty of stars in the shop window.

‌



Youri Tielemans was well known to United long before he took a prominent role for Belgium in North America. He isn't the only new face to arrive, with Andrey Santos, Karl Darlow and youngster Tynan Thompson all brought in.

‌



More players could be offloaded in order to free up space in Carrick's squad, with European football meaning more bodies are likely to be needed. We've taken a look at some of the World Cup standouts who could fit the bill.

‌



FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Man Utd ahead of Arsenal in Manu Kone race after opening transfer talks for £51m star READ MORE :

Michael Carrick issues next Man Utd transfer demand as Premier League stars targeted READ MORE :

Ayyoub Bouaddi

One of the most sought-after youngsters in global football at present, Bouaddi penned a fresh Lille contract last season - evidence that there was attention to fight off long before the World Cup. Judging by his standout display against Brazil, however, that new deal is unlikely to deter potential suitors.

United have prioritised younger targets in recent years and the 18-year-old midfielder certainly matches that profile. They also conducted recent business with Lille when they signed Leny Yoro in 2024.

‌



There will be hurdles, naturally. Bouaddi's performances have attracted interest from the likes of Manchester City and Paris Saint-Germain, both of whom boast substantial financial muscle and may bid more than United can spare right now.

Maxi Araujo

View 2 Images Maxi Araujo impressed at the World Cup despite Uruguay's struggles (Image: Michael Regan - FIFA, FIFA via Getty Images)

Araujo is familiar to former United manager Ruben Amorim, having featured under him at Sporting CP. Premier League supporters may recall the Uruguayan as the other goalscorer when a Viktor Gyokeres hat-trick propelled Sporting to a memorable Champions League triumph over Manchester City in 2024.

‌



The 26-year-old impressed despite his national team crashing out at the group stage. He contributed to all three goals from Marcelo Bielsa's side, netting twice and laying on a goal for Agustin Canobbio

Capable of playing at left-back or on the left wing, Araujo's adaptability could appeal to United. However, they may be wary of spending too much on a Sporting star with Gyokeres blowing hot and cold for Arsenal and Manuel Ugarte - also once of the Portuguese side - struggling in United red.

Antonio Nusa

Staying with wide options, Nusa has been linked with a Premier League switch for a number of years. At his first World Cup, the Norway winger demonstrated precisely why that's been the case.

‌



The 21-year-old was chiefly deployed on the left by Stale Solbakken, finding the net in the round of 32 triumph over Côte d'Ivoire. His ability to dovetail with Erling Haaland won't have gone unnoticed and it could be time to give him a chance in English football.

Nusa's youth means there's considerable room for growth. That said, current club RB Leipzig are unlikely to let him go on the cheap.

Manu Kone

United are already believed to be among the contenders for Kone as they aim to add one more central midfielder. The Roma man is anticipated to be available for just over £40m, enabling the Giallorossi to more than double their investment.

‌



Kone caught the eye during his outings for France and some believed he was underutilised by Didier Deschamps. The 25-year-old was left out of the starting XI for the semi-final against Spain and was unable to make up for lost time when he entered at the break.

The former Toulouse man previously attracted interest from the Premier League during his time at Borussia Monchengladbach, with United, Liverpool and Chelsea all thought to be admirers. Liverpool could yet emerge as rivals this summer too, should Michael Carrick's side fail to move swiftly.

Learn more £85 Fanatics Buy Now on Fanatics Product Description Manchester United have launched their new home kit for the 2026/27 season, i nspired by the club's heritage and featuring a classic polo collar with iconic adidas details.

‌



Ibrahim Mbaye

Paris Saint-Germain winger Mbaye represents another, younger wide option. Fabrizio Romano reported earlier this week that the teenager joined Jorge Mendes' agency in preparation for a summer transfer.

United have not yet been mentioned amongst his suitors but there's reason to believe he could be the profile of player they need. So far, Manchester City and Aston Villa have both shown interest in the Senegal star, who won't come at a bargain price but carries enormous potential at just 18 years of age.

Mbaye wasted no time in displaying his talent at the World Cup. He netted one of the standout strikes of the group stage, leaving Theo Hernandez sprawling with breathtaking footwork before outpacing Mike Maignan for a goal on his tournament debut.

‌



Yasin Ayari

Sweden star Ayari was another who caught the eye during the group stage. The 22-year-old struck two magnificent long-range efforts in a 5-1 thrashing of Tunisia, including his nation's opening goal of the tournament.

Premier League sides are well acquainted with the Brighton midfielder, who has already racked up more than 60 appearances in England's top flight. He was questioned about Liverpool speculation early in the World Cup but preferred to delay any discussion regarding his future.

"I'm in the World Cup bubble, as they say, and I don't have any control over anything," Ayari told Fotboll Skanalen. "Everyone else is taking care of it for me. I'm just here focusing on the World Cup."

Sports.title: Andoni Iraola now has something Arne Slot and Jurgen Klopp never did at Liverpool
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola now has something Arne Slot and Jurgen Klopp never did at Liverpool

Andoni Iraola has been in charge of Liverpool for a matter of weeks and has already enjoyed something not seen at Anfield since 2010

View 2 Images Andoni Iraola has plenty to work with in his first Liverpool season (Image: PETER POWELL, AFP via Getty Images)

Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola is just a few weeks into his tenure but already has something never enjoyed by Arne Slot or Jurgen Klopp. Not only that but it's something only present in one Reds season in the Premier League era.

‌



Thanks to new signing Victor Munoz's presence in Spain's victorious World Cup squad, Iraola has two World Cup winners at his disposal at the same time. You have to go back more than a decade for the last time that was the case.

‌



Munoz might not have played for La Roja at the tournament as he struggled with injury but the former Osasuna winger still has a winner's medal. Liverpool's other World Cup winner is of course Alexis Mac Allister, though the midfielder was still on Brighton's books when he started for Argentina in the 2022 final.

‌



It's also the first time ever that Liverpool have had two World Cup winners from different countries at the same time. The last time they had two world champions was in 2010, as Pepe Reina and Fernando Torres both won with Spain.

FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Torres didn't stick around for long, though. He joined Chelsea midway through the following season, leaving Reina as the sole survivor.

There's only one other example of the Reds having multiple World Cup winners at the same time. Roger Hunt, Ian Callaghan and Gerry Byrne were all part of the England squad that claimed the trophy on home turf in 1966 and were all Liverpool players when they achieved the feat.

View 2 Images Victor Munoz arrives fresh off a World Cup triumph (Image: Marvin Ibo Guengoer - GES Sportfoto, Getty Images)

‌



Munoz completed his £34m move during the World Cup as Liverpool beat Newcastle to a player who turned 23 during the tournament. "With Victor, I think we signed him in a moment where he's very hungry, he's ambitious, but he's still humble and knows that he has to come very ready," new boss Iraola said.

"I think he's someone with some versatility – can play right, can play left, he has the work-rate also for all that we will require. Looking forward to having him here, even if we know that we will have to wait with him and Macca."

Iraola is taking a 31-man squad to the United States for pre-season but Munoz and Mac Allister will both be afforded additional time off following their World Cup exertions. Liverpool have matches against Sunderland, Wrexham and Leeds on the other side of the Atlantic before heading back home for a pair of friendlies at Anfield in August.

Sports.title: Arsenal could boost transfer war chest by £90m with four exits in the works
Sports.content:
Arsenal could boost transfer war chest by £90m with four exits in the works

Arsenal could boost their transfer budget

View 3 Images Mikel Arteta is ready for a host of new arrivals (Image: Ryan Pierse/Getty Images)

Arsenal could increase their summer budget by at least £90million if players such as Gabriel Jesus and Ben White are offloaded. The Gunners have secured Piero Hincapie and Illan Meslier on permanent transfers with Christos Tzolis poised to become the third new arrival.

‌



Arsenal have invested £68.5m so far and Mikel Arteta will also seek to trim down his squad. Leandro Trossard has already left north London, moving to Besiktas for £15.3m.

‌



Jakub Kiwior has also departed, generating £14m following a successful loan spell at Porto that triggered a permanent transfer. The Gunners could strengthen their finances further with four additional transactions in the pipeline.

‌



Gabriel Jesus has been linked with a potential departure in recent weeks as the striker has just 12 months remaining on his deal. The Brazilian ranks among the highest-paid players in north London despite a recent shortage of playing time owing to injuries.

FOLLOW OUR ARSENAL FB PAGE! Latest Gunners news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Arsenal to receive millions in FIFA compensation after disastrous World Cup blow READ MORE :

The Athletic reports that the club values Jesus between £18m and £20m with Serie A outfit AC Milan having expressed interest. Calciomercato suggested that both parties could finalise a deal for approximately £16m with separate reports indicating that the Italian side are in discussions.

‌



Fellow Brazilian Gabriel Martinelli is also attracting transfer interest from several clubs, with Calciomercato reporting that Manchester United, Newcastle and Bayern Munich are all keeping tabs on the winger. It is understood that the Gunners will sanction a sale for £42.6m as they await the arrival of new signing Tzolis to fill his boots.

Experienced defender Ben White is another Arsenal figure touted for a departure. The 28-year-old managed just 12 Premier League appearances last season, with Jurrien Timber emerging as the preferred option at right-back.

3 View 3 Images Gabriel Martinelli and Gabriel Jesus are linked with exits (Image: Crystal Pix/MB Media/Getty Images) 3 View 3 Images Christian Norgaard and Ben White may also leave (Image: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

‌



Arsenal are believed to be holding out for a minimum of £25m for White, with Everton said to be keen on securing his signature. However, injuries to both Timber and William Saliba could scupper those plans, with the right-back likely to be called upon in the near term.

Finally, Christian Norgaard could net Arsenal an additional £4.2m. The Mail reports that Crystal Palace are weighing up a move for the 32-year-old midfielder.

It is suggested that Norgaard's Premier League experience could bolster the Eagles' midfield. The defensive midfielder is valued at around £4.2m and could be available at a reasonable price given that his contract is set to expire next summer.

Sports.title: Man Utd may have to change plans for two players after Marcus Rashford return
Sports.content:
Man Utd may have to change plans for two players after Marcus Rashford return

Marcus Rashford is set to return to Manchester United's first-team squad after Barcelona failed to activate a £26m permanent transfer clause

View 2 Images Marcus Rashford could yet play a part for Manchester United next season (Image: Getty Images)

Marcus Rashford's return to the Manchester United first-team squad could have significant implications for both Patrick Dorgu and Matheus Cunha. It has been a deeply frustrating summer for the Reds Devils' homegrown talent.

‌



The winger's coveted switch to Barcelona appears increasingly unlikely to come to fruition after the Catalan club failed to trigger a £26million clause in last campaign's loan agreement to secure his permanent transfer. United are seeking alternative permanent suitors, with Bayern Munich and Tottenham Hotspur amongst the clubs reportedly in the frame.

‌



The club are keen to offload his £325,000-a-week wages in order to safeguard their newly implemented pay structure. Yet with no permanent deal for the winger on the horizon, United could find themselves having little choice but to cut their losses and send him out on loan once more before the window shuts.

‌



Alternatively, United may have to concede they cannot permanently remove his wages from the books and bring him back into the first-team fold. There will be optimism at Old Trafford in that scenario that Carrick could unlock the best from the England international, much as he did with numerous players during his interim tenure last season.

Alejandro Garnacho set to swap places with Morgan Rogers as Aston Villa eye swoop READ MORE :

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

However, his reintegration into United's squad as another left-wing option will undoubtedly affect several key figures in Carrick's setup.

‌



Dorgu is one such player. The Danish wing-back found himself without a natural role in United's setup after Ruben Amorim's 3-4-2-1 formation was abandoned under Carrick.

Yet the 21-year-old demonstrated real potential in Rashford's left-wing berth, delivering eye-catching displays in memorable victories against Manchester City and Arsenal. The question remains whether he would be content with a reduced role having enjoyed so much game time under Carrick last term.

Rashford's comeback could equally affect Cunha, who served as United's primary left-wing option. The Brazilian made a strong impression with 10 goals and four assists, playing a pivotal part in the Reds' third-placed finish and their return to Champions League football.

‌



View 2 Images Patrick Dorgu could be impacted by Marcus Rashford's return (Image: 2026 Manchester United FC)

Cunha was not recruited as a squad player, though his form last season looks certain to secure him a starting spot at the very least heading into 2026/27. One possible solution for Carrick would be to utilise the 27-year-old as a centre-forward — a role he filled on several occasions last term — with Benjamin Sesko still sidelined with a shin injury.

BBC Sport reports that Rashford, who has two years left to run on his contract, is "relaxed" about the prospect of returning to train with the United squad. The 28-year-old is also understood to have a far more positive relationship with former teammate Carrick, in stark contrast to his "confrontational relationship" with ex-United boss Amorim.

‌



Rashford contributed 14 goals and 14 assists for Barcelona last season, claiming the La Liga title in the process. Following the conclusion of his World Cup duties, Rashford posted on social media with an optimistic message.

He said: "Keep believing in us. Our time will come. Now it's time for me to rest, reflect, spend some quality time with family and friends, and come back a better version of myself."

Sports.title: Man Utd only have room for two more specific signings as Premier League rule forces hand
Sports.content:
Man Utd only have room for two more specific signings as Premier League rule forces hand

Manchester United have already completed three transfers this summer but their future plans will have to revolve around league restrictions

View 2 Images Manchester United are working on more arrivals as the season draws closer (Image: Manchester United, Manchester United via Getty Images)

Manchester United have been busy this summer, adding Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans and Karl Darlow to their ranks. However, Premier League squad rules look like complicating their future plans unless they can make some sales.

‌



Santos and Tielemans arrived for more than £80m between them while Darlow joined on a free transfer from Leeds. There have also been exits - Casemiro and Andre Onana notable among them - but there could still be complications when it comes to naming their 25-man Premier League squad for the new season.

‌



League rules mean that 25-player allowance needs to be made up of 17 non-homegrown players and eight who qualify as homegrown. The latter category doesn't need to be players trained by United specifically - English and Welsh-trained players will also count, including new goalkeeper Darlow.

‌



Players aged 21 or under (born on or after January 1, 2005) don't get counted against either allowance but age threshold means United players born in 2004 no longer qualify as part of the Under-21 exemption for the 2026/27 season. Patrick Dorgu now takes up a non-homegrown slot, while Dan Gore and Toby Collyer occupy homegrown berths.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Man Utd ahead of Arsenal in Manu Kone race after opening transfer talks for £51m star READ MORE :

Michael Carrick issues next Man Utd transfer demand as Premier League stars targeted READ MORE :

Gore featured against Wrexham in Saturday's pre-season friendly but could still be moved on despite an impressive performance, as might Collyer after ending last season out on loan. Goalkeeper Radek Vitek - also classified as homegrown - is anticipated to depart despite appearing at the weekend.

‌



Alongside Dorgu, the non-homegrown group currently stands at 15 and features new arrivals Santos and Tielemans. The group is rounded out by Senne Lammens, Altay Bayındır, Noussair Mazraoui, Matthijs de Ligt, Lisandro Martínez, Diogo Dalot, Manuel Ugarte, Bruno Fernandes, Bryan Mbeumo, Matheus Cunha, Joshua Zirkzee and Benjamin Sesko.

To qualify as homegrown, a player does not need to be British as long as they have spent three seasons on an English or Welsh club's books by the end of the season in which they turn 21. This means winger Amad, who arrived at United as a teenager, is eligible to occupy one of the homegrown places.

View 2 Images Ivorian winger Amad qualifies as homegrown (Image: David Horton - CameraSport, CameraSport via Getty Images)

‌



Amad is among 11 homegrown players aged over 21, alongside the previously mentioned Gore, Collyer and Vitek as well as Tom Heaton, Karl Darlow, Harry Maguire, Luke Shaw, Mason Mount, Marcus Rashford and Dermot Mee. That said, a number of those individuals may well have moved on from Old Trafford before the campaign kicks off.

Vitek, Gore and Collyer are possibly the most likely to exit, with Vitek already indicating a desire for regular first-team football. Should all three depart, it would still leave United with eight homegrown players while freeing up two additional slots for non-homegrown recruits.

The non-homegrown quota could still rise. Bayindir may join fellow goalkeeper Onana in the Turkish Super Lig, while United might yet choose to omit Ugarte from their 25-man squad if his serious injury sustained on World Cup duty means he wouldn't play anyway.

‌



So, while the number of available places might appear limited at present, there is every possibility it can expand. There is already room for Manu Kone amid speculation linking the France midfielder, while new signing Tynan Thompson won't count towards any quota as he is under the age of 21.

Matters could become complicated should another one of those homegrown players depart, however, with Rashford amongst those with an uncertain future. More exits could potentially prompt United to sign another homegrown player if they wish to fulfil their complete quota of 25 players in their official Premier League squad.

Sports.title: Liverpool news: Bargain World Cup hero eyed as path opens to £80m Andoni Iraola transfer reunion
Sports.content:
Liverpool news: Bargain World Cup hero eyed as path opens to £80m Andoni Iraola transfer reunion

Liverpool's transfer odds have taken a serious turn for the better as Andoni Iraola chases a World Cup icon, while the possibility of an emotional reunion has emerged

View 2 Images Ferran Torres is reportedly a target for Liverpool after his World Cup final heroics (Image: FRANCK FIFE / AFP via Getty Images)

Transfer season is picking up at Anfield despite the fact Andoni Iraola's Liverpool are no longer in the building. The squad has jetted to the United States for its pre-season tour, which has coincided with a sudden spike of activity on the rumours front.

‌



Now that World Cup 2026 is done and dusted, fans can expect business to pick up in a big way. And Iraola is all but certain to be more active in the coming weeks as he gets to grips with the talents at his disposal.

‌



One World Cup star in particular looks destined to be on the move, with news that the Reds have entered the race. The ECHO has taken a deeper dive into that and more as the latest transfer headlines spell good news at Anfield.

‌



FOLLOW OUR LIVERPOOL FB PAGE! Latest Reds news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

Reds compete for World Cup hero Torres

Ferran Torres is reportedly being lined up for a return to the Premier League if Liverpool get their way. The news comes on the back of Spain's extra-time triumph over Argentina in Sunday's World Cup final, where he scored the only goal.

Alex Scott puts his foot down with Man Utd and Arsenal put on red alert for huge transfer READ MORE :

Barcelona winger Torres came off the bench to power La Roja over the finish line in New Jersey and write his name in the history books. And that finish may help in clinching a move to Anfield this summer.

‌



Paris Saint-Germain have been most closely linked with the player, as well as Liverpool wing target Yan Diomande. Added to the fact Les Parisiens already have Bradley Barcola, the Reds' other primary target for that position, and a showdown looks inevitable at some point this summer.

However, Torres would come a lot cheaper than those other two names given he's older and is now in the final 12 months of his contract at the Camp Nou. L'Equipe has reported Liverpool are ready to challenge PSG for his cut-price signature, which is allegedly valued somewhere between £40million and £50m.

That's less than half the kind of fees being associated with Diomande and Barcola. Meanwhile, Torres would arguably be a more natural fit given he's more accustomed to playing on the right flank, which is where the Reds have a Salah-shaped void.

It's been so long since Torres spent 18 months at Manchester City before departing for Barca in January 2022, yet he's still in his prime years after turning 26 in February. Why Barca aren't keen on extending the terms of a player who scored 21 goals in all competitions last season, only they will know, but the Catalans' loss could be Liverpool's gain.

In fact, Torres has averaged 20 goals per season across the past two campaigns for Barca and is an incredibly malleable asset, able to play off either wing or as a false nine. Add to that his advantage in experience having already played in the Premier League and his signature suddenly becomes that much more desirable.

Alex Scott reunion pathway cleared

View 2 Images Alex Scott has turned down a Bournemouth contract extension for the second time so far this year (Image: Robin Jones - AFC Bournemouth/AFC Bournemouth via Getty Images)

Alex Scott's chances of securing a move away from Bournemouth have increased after he turned down a new contract. It's reportedly the second time in 2026 the English playmaker has rejected fresh terms at the Vitality Stadium.

Scott, 22, formed a strong connection with Iraola during their time together on the south coast. The new Liverpool chief has spoken highly of Scott in the past and would possess a key advantage in any bidding war to snag his services.

Article continues below

Sky Sports News reported Manchester United, Arsenal and Chelsea are ahead of Liverpool in the hunt. And midfield doesn't appear to be a major priority for Liverpool right now, particularly given there's greater need for new faces down the right side.

However, with just two years remaining on his contract, this could be the big opportunity to get Scott on board if Iraola desires. The former Bristol City star is purportedly valued at north of £80m, with Bournemouth facing a dilemma over whether to capitalise now or risk losing their star for a heavily reduced fee in future.

Sports.title: Man Utd news: £60m star rejects new contract as 'calls and texts' to transfer target emerge
Sports.content:
Man Utd news: £60m star rejects new contract as 'calls and texts' to transfer target emerge

Manchester United have been given a boost regarding their summer transfer business

View 3 Images Alex Scott has given United a boost (Image: Getty)

Manchester United's rebuild under Michael Carrick is in full effect. The new permanent United boss has already welcomed several new signings as the club prepares to face Norwegian side Rosenborg on Friday in their second pre-season fixture.

‌



So far, Andrey Santos has joined from Chelsea before the club pulled off a stunning move for Aston Villa's Youri Tielemans. Joining those two is former veteran goalkeeper Karl Darlow, who has signed from Leeds.

‌



United's move for highly rated Tottenham prospect Tynan Thompson shows they're also considering their long-term future. The latest news, however, focuses on a potential exit for United, while, elsewhere, the club have been given a boost over another summer transfer target.

‌



United star receiving 'texts and calls' over move

United forward Joshua Zirkzee has been of interest to Juventus, as the Serie A side weighs up a move for the Dutch star. Zirkzee has long been linked with a return to Italy after struggling to light up the Premier League since arriving at Old Trafford in 2024 for £36.5million from Bologna.

While he has only scored five goals in 56 Premier League appearances, the 25-year-old's stock in Italy seems to have remained high. Gazetta dello Sport report that Juventus CEO Giovanni Carnevali and sporting director Marco Ottolini are looking to replace Dusan Vlahovic, who was recently released.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Paul Scholes accuses Thomas Tuchel of trying to get sacked after comments on England stars READ MORE :

Zirkzee is believed to have been on the receiving end of 'texts, calls and video calls' as the Serie A giants enquired over his availability. Juve's preference is believed to be PSG's Kolo Muani, but their £34m bid has not yet been accepted as the Parisians look to hold out for more.

View 3 Images Joshua Zirkzee is one player who could leave Manchester United this summer. (Image: Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images)

Zirkzee started United's opening pre-season match of the summer and failed to find the net as Carrick's team fell to defeat against Wrexham. In April, it was reported that Zirkzee was 'intent' on staying at Old Trafford beyond the summer, but it looks like he could be on the move.

‌



Alex Scott boost

United may have been handed a boost in their chase for Alex Scott after he rejected a new contract offer from Bournemouth. The 22-year-old has been strongly linked with a move to Old Trafford this summer.

The Cherries have Scott tied down to a contract until 2028 and have tried to extend his terms. However, according to Sky Sports, he is not currently willing to accept those, with his camp having rejected a fresh deal.

View 3 Images Alex Scott is a main target for United (Image: Visionhaus/Getty Images)

‌



A release clause for Scott has been reported, but with nothing signed, Scott is expected to cost any admirers around £60m.

United's pursuit of the midfielder comes as Carrick is said to be looking for a third addition to the engine room. Scott appears to be the concrete option, alongside AS Roma's Manu Kone.

Scott's club team-mate, Tyler Adams, has also been linked with a move to Old Trafford. Arsenal have been linked with Scott too, but Newcastle United's Bruno Guimaraes seems to be their priority target.

Hilltop, Kaori and Mojito contest a trappy-looking Download The At The Races App Fillies' Handicap at Lingfield.

Harry Hope looks a danger for the Ben Pauling and Jones combination. He has an excellent strike-rate over fences and should strip fitter for his last outing at Stratford.

Axel Bleue scored over this track and trip 21 days ago and remains unexposed over fences.

Sports.title: Red Bull getting calls from 'good drivers' over future seat - Mekies
Sports.content:
Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies has suggested they are getting calls from "good drivers" about potential future seats at the team but believes they will make the further pace improvements required to ensure Max Verstappen stays.

As Formula 1 prepares for its final race before the summer break in Hungary this weekend, Verstappen's Red Bull future beyond this season remains uncertain.

His contract runs to the end of the 2028 season but contains performance clauses that would allow him to leave at the end of this year. He is thought to have until October to inform the team should he wish to activate a break in the deal.

It emerged last month that the Dutchman's representatives had spoken with McLaren, although the latter's Zak Brown has subsequently made clear that "I've got my two drivers" in Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri. Mercedes and Ferrari's drivers are also under contract, seemingly limiting Verstappen's short-term options beyond Red Bull, should he first choose to stay in F1, into 2027.

With it considered normal that Verstappen's representatives would be keeping abreast of potential options for their driver elsewhere, Mekies was asked by Sky Sports F1 at the Belgian Grand Prix whether his team, in turn, had also received enquiries from drivers elsewhere on the grid.

"It's working in both directions," replied Mekies. "It's completely natural and I think that's what you guys were reporting before.

"It's completely natural Max gets called from everyone because he's the best driver in the world and, equally, if you are a top team, you are going to get calls from many of these good drivers around as well. That's natural.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ahead of the Belgian Grand Prix, Max Verstappen gave blunt responses to questions about his future at Red Bull.

"Is it a distraction for us? Not really. The full focus is to get that car as fast as it can, then you will keep your best driver in the world and we also see there's a massive growth of Isack [Hadjar] alongside Max.

"That for us is the ideal pairing and we try to make sure we can keep that pairing."

Mekies is confident Red Bull will deliver on their ongoing quest to close its remaining gap to the front of the field after steps forward since the start of the season in F1's new era of regulations.

Since a big upgrade of the RB22 three races ago at the Austrian Grand Prix, Verstappen has finished on the podium in two of the last three races, although endured a difficult Silverstone where he spun out late on due to a rear-wing fault.

Isack Hadjar finished sixth from 21st on the grid last weekend in Belgium to extend his run of top-six finishes to six races.

"All we need to do is to continue to progress with the car," said Mekies.

"We started the season a bit more than one second off the pace and I don't think we should be surprised at that.

"I think it's a product of how late the title push was last year - a product of how late the title push was last year, a product of the incredible challenge of the new power unit.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player After finishing third in Belgium, Max Verstappen has disputed the FIA rating Red Bull's engine as the benchmark in Formula One.

"We started on the back foot but these guys did it again. We were more than a second away and we are now talking about the last two or three tenths for ultimate pace.

"When you are one second away, the drivers are going to be frustrated, Max is going to be frustrated. And we know it's not the position we want to stay.

"To your point, the best way to close the subject is to go and get these last two or three tenths and that's what everyone is focused on."

Red Bull have seen the departure of a number of key figures associated with their past title-winning successes over the last two years, while Verstappen's own race engineer and key ally, Gianpiero Lambiase, is heading to McLaren no later than 2028.

Asked how that sense of 'transition' at the team marries with attempts to keep Verstappen, Mekies said: "It's more simple than what it seems, because ultimately it's only about speed.

"Red Bull and Red Bull Racing only have one objective, it's to win, and it's the same objective that Max has.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Belgian Grand Prix.

"So, it's not about, how can we prove to him that we can win. We are here to win anyhow.

"It's the same group of people that have done the incredible turnaround last year, that was a few months ago. It's the same group of people that, despite that late push, has managed to absorb nearly one second off our competitors, and they were not waiting for us in these first races.

"Now we are in the hardcore part of it, the last few tenths, the most difficult ones to get, but what we need to do is continue to work as a united group, and that's how we'll produce the best results."
