World.title: Turkish Airlines suspected of using Russian airspace on flight from Tallinn
World.content:
A Turkish Airlines aircraft operating a passenger flight from Tallinn to Istanbul on 12 July allegedly ended up over Russian territory during the flight.

The aircraft changed its usual route and flew over the Kaliningrad region, although flights normally avoid Russian airspace, writes the online edition of the weekly Eesti Ekspress.

One passenger said he noticed the route change in a flight‑tracking app and approached a flight attendant. After consulting the pilots, he was told that flying over Kaliningrad was a deliberate decision by the crew, as they considered this route the most optimal.

Lennuliiklusteeninduse AS, the company responsible for air‑traffic management in Estonia, said that according to the approved flight plan, the route should have passed through Latvia, Lithuania, Poland, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria, without entering Russian airspace.

The head of the aviation department at Estonia's Ministry of Climate, Taivo Linnamägi, emphasized that flights over Russian territory are considered unsafe for civil aviation due to the ongoing war and the risks associated with it.

Although Turkish Airlines has the right to use Russian airspace, Flightradar data shows that such a route is rather an exception for flights between Tallinn and Istanbul.

Representatives of Turkish Airlines have not commented the incident, Eesti Ekspress said.

World.title: Mihkel Mariusz Jezierski: Students expect clear rules for using AI
World.content:
Discussions held with roughly a thousand Estonian high school students revealed one important conclusion: the need for clearer agreements on the use of artificial intelligence in learning. Uncertainty is students' biggest concern, writes Mihkel Mariusz Jezierski.

From March to May, 950 high school students in 18 Estonian schools took part in world‑café discussions about the role of artificial intelligence in school and its impact on learning, relationships, creativity, social‑media use and their sense of the future.

In Estonia, discussions often focus on how AI affects learning, but much less on how it affects education as a whole: relationships, creativity, the information environment and perceptions of the future. School is not only a place where knowledge is acquired, but an environment where a person develops. Therefore, the role of AI must be assessed much more broadly than through learning outcomes alone.

Although students are the first to experience AI's impact every day, they are rarely included in discussions about what role AI should have in school. The world‑café sessions aimed to fill that gap.

Uncertainty creates unfairness

Students say that schools and teachers differ greatly in how they handle AI use. Some teachers ban AI entirely, while others actively encourage it. Students feel a sense of unfairness — and reduced trust in teacher‑created materials — when a teacher uses AI to create learning materials but forbids students from using the same tool.

Uncertainty also creates unfairness in assessment, students say. They described situations where independently completed work received a lower grade than work done with AI, because the teacher found it difficult to distinguish the student's contribution from AI's. When a grade no longer reflects a student's actual knowledge or effort, assessment loses part of its meaning in students' eyes.

"They described situations where independently completed work received a lower grade than work done with AI."

A similar uncertainty concerns creative work. Only 21 percent of students believe that a result created with AI is fully their own. Creativity is often tied to self‑determination and a sense of ownership. Many high school students want clear guidance on how to use AI in ways that support idea development without replacing the creative process or becoming the source of ideas itself. They also need instructions on how to describe and cite AI's contribution in their work.

For this reason, students expect to work with teachers to write down agreements that define when, how and to what extent AI may be used in learning. One of the goals of the AI‑Leap student program for the next school year is to help shape such shared agreements in every Estonian school.

The AI‑Leap initiative does not aim to restrict AI use, but to help find solutions that support learning and keep school primarily a human‑created environment rather than one shaped around technology.

Exclusion may encourage misuse of AI

AI provides quick, non‑judgmental answers. For many students, it is easier to turn to AI than to a teacher, parent or peer — especially when they fear making mistakes. It turned out that about one‑third of high school students seek help from AI first when a problem arises, although one‑fifth do so rarely or have never turned to AI.

Students say misuse of chatbots occurs more often among peers who have mental‑health concerns or difficulties with communication. The weaker the emotional support and sense of belonging, the more likely a young person is to replace normal interaction with AI.

At the same time, high school students emphasize that AI should not and cannot replace a human as a communication partner. They see the solution in strengthening the school's social role: because AI makes learning increasingly individual, schools should support communication and community feeling more than before and ensure mental‑health support.

I believe that AI's impact on education should not be assessed only through learning outcomes. School is where relationships, belonging and young people themselves take shape. The more individual AI makes learning, the more important it is to keep school a human‑designed environment.

Personalized learning must not make school more lonely

AI enables more personalized learning than before, but we must ask how this affects students' relationships, cooperation and sense of belonging when each learner moves increasingly along their own individual learning path together with AI.

Educational technology should not personalize only learning — it should also help maintain the relationships and shared experiences through which a school becomes a community. This does not have to hinder innovation. But these are principles that must be considered in developing any AI solution for education, including further development of AI‑Leap's Socratic learning application ITI.

The world‑café discussions also highlighted concerns about social‑media algorithms, which students say increasingly shape their worldview and information consumption. Young people also feel uncertainty about the future, because AI is changing the labor market and required skills. They want schools to teach more media literacy, the principles behind algorithms, and skills for adapting to a rapidly changing world.

High school students' message to their schools is that above all they expect the opportunity to formulate clear agreements on AI use together with teachers. They also consider important a school culture that values making mistakes and learning from them, accessible mental‑health support, individual feedback, and transparent labeling of AI use.

World.title: 19th century Estonian settlers in Caucasus linked malaria to hard work, raw berries
World.content:
An Estonian National Museum (ERM) expert has shed light on how Estonian settlers in the Caucasus region dealt with the scourge of malaria, at a time when the illness was poorly understood.

Estonians settled primarily along the Black Sea coast of the Caucasus region, including in Abkhazia, in the late 19th to early 20th centuries. Like Estonia itself, the area was part of the Tsarist Empire before World War One.

At the time, malaria, a deadly disease, was not fully understood and while quinine was available, sometimes folk remedies were chosen ahead of it by the Estonian arrivals.

Whereas today, the fact that malaria gets spread by mosquitoes is common knowledge, anti-malarial tablets were some decades off and many Estonians who moved to the Caucasus region over a century ago blamed the deadly disease on damp ground, raw berries or even excessive hard work.

The new overview has been assembled by ERM senior researcher Aivar Jürgenson, who studied settlers' correspondence, memoirs and newspaper articles from the late 19th to early 20th centuries, prior to Estonia's independence. His findings were reported also in the journal Philological Researches.

Caucasus Estonians in nature. Source: RA/EFA.505.0.154300

Soon after the villages of Linda, Estonia, Salme and Sulevi were established by Estonian settlers in Abkhazia in the 1880s, malaria became one of the deadliest enemies for the new residents.

More than half of the arriving emigrants contracted the disease and were taken seriously ill, and nearly 16 percent of the settlements' populations died of malaria.

Because science had not at that time discovered the connection between mosquitoes and malaria, the settlers believed in prevailing theories of the time. According to these, malaria emanated as a poisonous vapor from damp ground and swamps. To combat this, houses began to be built on stilts, so that air might pass beneath the floors. Eucalyptus trees were planted to dry the ground, and swamps were drained. Since this deprived mosquitoes of their breeding grounds, this did serve to curb the incidence of malaria, albeit not for the reasons understood.

Descriptions also revealed the impact malaria had on a central tenet of Estonian national pride: Namely the work ethic. Obviously those suffering from malaria could not work, but the arrivals had also seen local inhabitants as "lazy." When ethnic Estonians started falling ill too, another misguided conclusion emerged – the belief that a person from northerly climes simply could not withstand strenuous labor in a hotter climate.

Only later was it grasped that it was malaria itself that was exhausting people. The folly of eating raw berries and drinking water which had not been boiled first were soon added to the supposed list of causes of malaria.

Malaria is carried by mosquitoes, though this was not understood in the late 19th century. Source: Egor Kamelev/Unsplash

As well as the attributed causes, the methods used to treat malaria at the time reveal a colorful blend of folk tradition and contemporary medicine. Imported from Estonia was another belief: That malaria was a spirit in the shape of a gray old man that had to be driven away or frightened. For this reason, the malaise was known as "Halltõbi" ("Gray disease").

Supposed cures included rolling around in the straw in a pigsty, or keeping pieces of crosses collected from cemeteries under the left side of the body while sleeping.

The properties of quinine, originally from the New World, were known about by this time, at least to medical professionals, and doctors did start prescribing this plant-based treatment.

However, many Estonian arrivals not only found quinine's bitter taste – familiar to many today in tonic water, which it is a key ingredient of – unpalatable, they also mistakenly believed that the medicine was poisonous, opting to consume locally made wine instead in an effort to cure the disease's ravages.

Malaria still exists and WHO data states in 2024 there were around 282 million malaria cases, and 610,000 deaths as a result of the disease, chiefly in Africa.

Symptoms can be both mild and life-threatening. Mild symptoms include fever, chills and headache. Severe symptoms include fatigue, confusion, seizures, and difficulty breathing. Prophylactic medicines can be taken ahead of visiting a region known to have cases of malaria, and care should be taken to avoid mosquito bites, including by using repellents and netting.

World.title: 3 drones intercepted near US consulate in northern Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi security sources said on Tuesday that air defenses intercepted three explosive-laden drones near the US consulate in Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq, according to Reuters.

A separate source told Al-Arabiya News that two drones targeted a camp of the Kurdistan Freedom Party (PAK), an Iranian Kurdish opposition group.

No casualties or damage resulting from the drone attack in Erbil have been reported.

The state-run news agency (INA) reported that Erbil International Airport temporarily suspended flights but later announced their resumption.

Iraqi air defenses shot down an explosive-laden drone on Monday near Harir Air Base in Iraq, which houses US and international coalition forces. There were no reports of casualties or damages.

During the Middle East war, Iran and its allied Iraqi militias have targeted Iraqi Kurdistan, which hosts US soldiers as part of the international coalition fighting ISIS, foreign oil firms, and Iranian Kurdish opposition parties.

The recent escalation in Iraqi Kurdistan, which largely included drone assaults over Erbil, comes amid rising tensions between the United States and Iran, the most serious since a cease-fire deal was reached in mid-June.

World.title: AI boom lifts Mexico tech exports, complicating Trump trade goals
World.content:
Mexico City – The United States’ frenzied rush to build out AI infrastructure has boosted exports of Mexican technology, complicating President Donald Trump’s hand heading into trade negotiations.

Trump, who campaigned on boosting US manufacturing, hopes to narrow the trade deficit with Mexico during talks to update the USMCA free trade agreement, which kick off Tuesday in Mexico City.

But the dizzying rise in computer equipment exports from Mexico — the largest US trading partner — is doing the opposite.

Between January and April, Mexico tripled its sales of computer equipment to the United States compared to the same period last year, with exports topping $50 billion versus just $2.2 billion in imports, according to AFP calculations.

The sector now makes up 30 percent of all Mexican products shipped to the United States, overtaking the automotive industry as the largest component of exports.

“It’s a milestone largely driven by demand for advanced AI electronics,” Diego Flores, head of electronic and digital industries at Mexico’s Economy Ministry, told AFP.

The sector, which includes processing units and data center hardware, is not officially on the agenda for this round of negotiations.

– Explosive demand –

The most in-demand products are server racks that house AI processing cards — a key component for the data centers multiplying across the United States.

The main export hub is the Pacific state of Jalisco, dubbed the “Mexican Silicon Valley,” where an ecosystem of global industry giants and tech startups have set up shop, Flores said.

Taiwanese giant Foxconn assembles server racks in Jalisco, and serves as a strategic partner to US chip designer Nvidia.

In March, Foxconn announced $137 million in investments across two Mexican subsidiaries after estimating its production could double this year.

“The United States and Mexico will remain our primary production hubs,” Chief Executive Michael Chiang said, announcing the company would invest 30 percent more than in 2025 to expand its AI-related capacity.

Faced with booming demand, Flextronics, another tech manufacturer in Jalisco, even had to repurpose its parking lots to expand manufacturing capacity, Flores said.

Yet the boom comes amid a volatile political climate.

The Trump administration rejected a 16-year extension of the USMCA, opting instead for annual reviews with Mexico and Canada.

Washington is also continuing to push for more goods to be manufactured domestically, even as US reliance on imports from Mexico, Taiwan, and China to fuel its AI boom grows.

– ‘In the line of fire’ –

Could the thriving sector become Trump’s next tariff target?

“Nobody can say for sure,” Flores admitted. However, he expressed confidence that the sector might escape protectionist policies due to its immense strategic value to the United States.

Washington is also seeking to limit the use of Asian technology within North America, according to William Jackson, a chief emerging markets economist at Capital Economics.

“The Trump administration has to weigh the demand for these technologies and the need to stay at the forefront of AI development,” he told AFP, noting that “tariffs could prove counterproductive to that goal.”

But balancing the preservation of a booming industry with protectionist rhetoric puts the sector “very easily in the line of fire,” he warned.

That risk is heightened by the fact that Mexican manufacturers use components sourced from China and Taiwan, which Trump could view as a “backdoor” or Trojan horse for Asian technology entering the United States.

World.title: At least 41 dead in Guyana capsized ferry disaster
World.content:
Georgetown – At least 41 people died after a ferry capsized off the coast of Guyana over the weekend, the government said Tuesday.

The MV Barima was traveling from the capital Georgetown to Port Kaituma in Guyana’s inland Essequibo region when it flipped over on Saturday night.

A desperate search for survivors has been underway since early Sunday, with 77 people rescued so far and dozens more missing, according to authorities.

A government report released Tuesday revised the death toll from 27 to 41.

“A total of 41 bodies have now been recovered,” it stated.

“The first recovery for the day was made at 10:15 am (1415GMT), and 14 bodies have been retrieved as of 1 pm” Tuesday, it added.

There had earlier been confusion over how many were involved in the tragedy due to an inaccurate passenger manifest which listed 133 people aboard, Public Works Minister Juan Edghill said.

But on Tuesday, Prime Minister Mark Phillips said he was confident that 179 people had been on board when the accident occurred.

Two crew members aboard the aging ferry tested positive for marijuana after the incident, he told reporters Sunday, adding that an investigation was underway.

The ship began its journey in mid-afternoon and a distress call was received about eight hours later.

The ferry was built in 1939, according to the shipping website VesselFinder.

Boats typically travel by sea before reaching a river to arrive at Port Kaituma, which is located in the depths of a dense rainforest.

Guyana, a small English-speaking country at the northeast corner of South America, is locked in a territorial dispute with neighboring Venezuela over the oil-rich Essequibo region.

World.title: Iraqi Airways launches new digital data center for automation push
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The management of Iraqi Airways has officially opened a new digital Data Center, marking a major step forward in its comprehensive digital transformation and electronic automation project.

Ahmed Abbas, Director of the Data Center, emphasized that the project builds upon the airline’s broader automation strategy. This plan aims to implement electronic systems across all company divisions and establish an integrated digital ecosystem.

By connecting all departments, branches, and operational units under a single, unified data center, the initiative will enhance information security, unify data management, boost operational efficiency, and ensure the sustainability of digital services.

Key Strategic Objectives

Core Digital Infrastructure: Serves as one of the airline’s most critical infrastructure upgrades, modernizing IT operations to align with global standards.

Accelerated Operations: Streamlines procedures, supports integrated electronic systems, and speeds up daily operational workflows.

Enhanced Service Quality: Leverages modern technology to elevate overall service standards and customer experiences.

Government Alignment: Fulfills national e-governance mandates and Council of Ministers decisions regarding digital transformation and infrastructure development.

By launching this centralized Data Center, Iraqi Airways continues to modernize its civil aviation infrastructure, bringing faster processing, improved security, and higher-quality digital services to both internal operations and passengers.

World.title: Trump ‘not finished’ with Iran as Tehran steps up strikes
World.content:
Tehran – President Donald Trump said Tuesday that the United States was not finished attacking Iran, as Tehran stepped up its strikes across the Middle East.

The US leader projected that it would take the Islamic republic more than 20 years to rebuild from damage sustained in the Middle East war, two weeks after fighting between the decades-old foes resumed.

“If we left right now, it would take Iran 20, 25 years to rebuild,” he said. “We’re not finished at all… we’re not leaving right now.”

His comments came after Jordan, Kuwait and Bahrain came under attack Tuesday.

Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels meanwhile said they would blockade Saudi Arabia’s ports, threatening to throw energy markets into chaos after Iran’s Strait of Hormuz blockade.

Bahrain said it intercepted Iranian attacks as sirens sounded multiple times in the kingdom, with Kuwait and Jordan also announcing they had intercepted drone and missile strikes.

Kuwait has said that Tehran hit multiple power and water desalination plants across the country over the past days, including on Monday, forcing residents to ration energy consumption.

Iran’s Guards confirmed a strike on Jordan, claiming they had targeted a “complex housing US terrorist forces in the region of Rukban”.

The Iranian army had earlier said it targeted US assets in Kuwait and Bahrain, including air defence systems, radar installations and administrative buildings.

“With this radar sweep, the enemy should prepare for even more decisive and powerful waves of drone and missile attacks,” the Guards said in a statement carried by state news agency IRNA.

– Houthi threat –

US President Donald Trump said he would “take care of” the Houthi rebels if the Iran-backed militant group followed through on its threatened blockade of Saudi ports.

“If something like that happens, we take care of it,” Trump said. “You know, we’ve done that with the Houthis before, and we haven’t heard from them in a while since we did what we did originally.”

Saudi Arabia strongly condemned the threat from what it called the “terrorist Houthi militia” and said it “continues to support the brotherly Yemeni people and their legitimate government”.

It remains unclear how the Houthis would implement their blockade of Saudi ports, and oil markets eased slightly despite the threat from Iran’s ally against the world’s biggest crude exporter.

But maritime intelligence provider Vanguard Tech said a Singapore-flagged tanker and a Liberia-flagged tanker both “reversed course” in the Red Sea after loading crude at the Saudi port of Yanbu following the Houthi warning.

Should the Houthis make good on their threat to blockade Saudi ports, that would put at risk Riyadh’s ability to bypass Hormuz for some of its oil exports and have major repercussions for the global economy.

Saudi Arabia and the Houthis traded fire last week for the first time in years, threatening a 2022 truce in their years-long conflict, but the rebels have largely remained on the sidelines since Israel and the US attacked Iran in late February.

The Revolutionary Guards said on Tuesday that two tankers attempting to transit Hormuz “were hit by explosions, resulting in massive fires that brought them to a standstill”.

The UK Maritime Trade Operations agency (UKMTO) earlier reported that an “unknown projectile” struck a tanker off the coast of Oman.

– ‘Still struggling’ –

Following the deaths of at least three US soldiers in recent days, the US launched a new round of attacks against Iran on Monday it said was “designed to further degrade Iranian military capabilities used to attack commercial shipping” in the Strait of Hormuz.

The deaths bring to 17 the number of fatalities among US service members. Nearly 100 US service members have been wounded since war resumed on July 7, the Pentagon said Monday.

Shahin, a 34-year-old embroiderer from Iranshahr in southeast Iran, said: “We’re still struggling to secure our most basic life necessities, and now we’re dealing with destruction from the war on top of it.”

As Iran stepped up its attacks in the Gulf, Kuwait’s foreign ministry on Tuesday said it had summoned Iran’s ambassador over a strike against a ship passing through the Hormuz strait the day before.

Despite the latest fighting, Iranian foreign ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said diplomatic exchanges with Washington via mediators were ongoing.

Mediator Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called for restraint from all warring sides during a meeting with Iran’s Interior Minister Eskandar Momeni on Tuesday.

Sharif urged the sides to “refrain from actions that could further destabilise the region”, his office said.

World.title: E-payment firms to assist CBI in driving Iraq’s digital transition
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Governor of the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) Nizar Hussein met on Tuesday with representatives of licensed electronic payment companies to enhance their role in supporting the country’s digital transformation.

The meeting addressed the role of e-payment firms in carrying out the CBI’s strategy to develop the electronic payments system and enhance financial inclusion.

Hussein noted that in the next term, electronic payment firms must improve the services provided to customers while adhering to the highest quality standards.

The step will boost public trust in electronic payment systems, foster the development of new digital payment solutions, reduce dependency on cash, and develop the digital economy, according to a statement released by the CBI.

Hussein urged electronic payment firms to adhere to international standards governing international financial transactions to open up more chances for sector development, boost card limitations, and introduce new financial services that match residents’ requirements.

The meeting addressed procedures that the CBI would adopt with electronic payment firms to eliminate card misuse, improve the security of the payment system, boost operational limitations, and offer advanced services to residents.

Hussein also called for increasing collaborations with CBI-licensed banks to achieve financial sector integration and develop a modern, secure, and innovative payment system.

World.title: Indian Oil Corp stops loading Iraqi oil amid Hormuz instability
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Sources told Reuters that Indian Oil Corp. (IOC) has stopped loading Iraqi oil from Basrah Oil Terminal due to increasing risk and assaults on vessels crossing the Strait of Hormuz.

Around July 23, the state-run IOC planned to transport 2 million barrels of Iraqi oil via the mega-sized crude carrier Lila Jamnagar.

Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals Ltd, a different state refiner, has also halted plans to transport oil from Iraq via the Indian-flagged Aframax tanker Desh Gaurav.

Following the resumption of military operations in the Strait of Hormuz, India has advised shipping companies to refrain from assigning Indian seafarers to vessels operating in that region.

Ship captains were also advised to be cautious regarding security in the Arabian Gulf, the Strait of Hormuz, and surrounding waterways and to continuously check navigational warnings.

Prior to the war, the Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman served as the primary transit route for around a fifth of the world’s oil and gas supplies.

Tensions have escalated since the truce between Washington and Tehran was broken in early July. This breakdown has resulted in attacks that have disrupted trade through the crucial waterway.

World.title: Turkish Transport Minister arrives in baghdad to elevate transport ties and Development Road cooperation
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Turkish Minister of Transport and Infrastructure Abdulkadir Uraloğlu arrived in Baghdad on Tuesday, July 21, 2026, to conduct high-level talks with Iraqi officials aimed at taking bilateral cooperation in transport, logistics, and telecommunications to a higher level.

Minister Uraloğlu was officially welcomed at Baghdad International Airport by Deputy Minister of Transport Hazem Razi Lafta, before holding bilateral talks with Iraqi Minister of Transport Wahb Al-Hasani at the state guesthouse in Baghdad.

Strategic Focus: The Development Road Project Primary Agenda: Fast-tracking execution phases of the multi-billion-dollar Development Road project, an international rail and highway network linking Grand Faw Port in southern Iraq directly to Turkey and European commercial markets.

Diplomatic Context: The visit serves as a key logistical precursor ahead of Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi’s upcoming official state visit to Turkey scheduled for July 28, 2026.

The visit underscores the massive economic weight and trade synergy between the two neighboring nations:

Heavy Commercial Volume: Bilateral trade volume between Iraq and Turkey stands at approximately $15 billion to $17 billion annually, with joint diplomatic initiatives aiming to expand total trade to $24 billion.

Key Trading Partner: Iraq consistently ranks among Turkey’s top export destinations globally (exceeding $12 billion in Turkish exports alone), primarily spanning food products, construction materials, machinery, and consumer goods.

Infrastructure Footprint: Turkish construction firms have historically undertaken over 1,100 development projects in Iraq valued at more than $36 billion, making Iraq one of the largest markets for Turkish engineering and infrastructure expertise worldwide.

By coordinating transport routes and cross-border digital networks through the Development Road project, both Baghdad and Ankara aim to secure long-term transit revenue, streamline regional supply chains, and further integrate their high-volume trade partnership.

World.title: NEET protest: Rahul Gandhi, opposition wear black in Parliament day after PM residence protest- watch
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Leader of opposition in the Lok Sabha

, along with MPs from the INDIA bloc, arrived in Parliament on Wednesday dressed in black to mark a "Black Day" over the alleged NEET irregularities and the police action against protesting students.

Congress MP

, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav, Trinamool Congress MP Mahua Moitra, JMM MP Mahua Maji and several other opposition leaders also wore black as they gathered at Makar Dwar to stage a protest on the third day of Monsoon session of Parliament. The MPs raised slogans demanding justice for students and the resignation of Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the controversy surrounding the examination.

Opposition reacts

Akhilesh Yadav questioned why the government was unwilling to remove the Union education minister, asking,"What pressure is the government under that it cannot remove the minister?" Explaining the Opposition's decision to wear black in Parliament, he said,"We have come wearing black clothes. Black is the colour of protest; it is also the colour of grief."

JMM MP Mahua Maji, while talking to reporters, said that the goal was to protect students, not score political points.





"Opposition stands unitedâ, she said.

Congress leaders Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and Mallikarjun Kharge also launched a sharp attack on the Centre during the Opposition's "Black Day" protest in Parliament.

Speaking to reporters, Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra said the focus should remain on the students' demands rather than the treatment meted out to Opposition leaders. "What happened with us is irrelevant. Students have genuine demands and are asking for their rights," she said.

She alleged that despite an education budget of Rs 1.4 lakh crore, the government had "waived off Rs 16 lakh crore loans for Adani and Ambani," while students continued to face repeated paper leaks. "Students have a genuine struggle and are asking for change. Paper leaks are happening repeatedly. There is nothing undemocratic about peaceful protest, but what is happening with students and in Parliament is undemocratic," she added.

Congress president and leader of opposition in the Rajya Sabha Mallikarjun Kharge also accused the Centre of undermining democratic institutions. "They are functioning like a dictatorship. They do not respect MPs. They harass even those who protest as per rules," he said.

Kharge further alleged that BJP-RSS workers were operating alongside the police and warned the government against attempting to intimidate the opposition.

World.title: 'Does India run on your arrogance?' BJP tears into Rahul Gandhi over PM residence march
World.content:
BJP calls Rahul's march to PM residence 'irresponsible conduct'

NEW DELHI: A day after Rahul Gandhi's march to Prime Minister Narendra Modi's residence ended in a confrontation with police, the BJP mounted a sharp political counteroffensive on Wednesday, accusing Lok Sabha leader of opposition of disregarding the dignity of the Prime Minister's residence and announcing nationwide protests against Congress party.The saffron party also called out Rahul Gandhi's "Chalo PM Residence" as "irresponsible" and "highly condemnable." Leading the attack, senior party leader Ravi Shankar Prasad asked Lok Sabha LoP: "'Does this country run on your arrogance?"Addressing a presser in New Delhi, senior BJP leader and former Union minister Ravi Shankar Prasad took a swipe at Rahul Gandhi's political legacy, saying that someone from a family that produced three Prime Ministers should have understood the dignity attached to the Prime Minister's residence."He is sitting on a dharna at the gate of the Prime Minister's residence. His father Rajiv Gandhi was the Prime Minister, his grandmother Indira Gandhi was the Prime Minister, and his great-grandfather Jawaharlal Nehru was also the Prime Minister of India. He, of all people, should know the dignity and sanctity of the Prime Minister's residence. Despite this, the kind of irresponsible behaviour he has displayed is highly condemnable," Prasad said.Announcing the BJP's response, Prasad said the saffron party would stage protests across the country outside Congress offices."The BJP will hold protests today across the country against Congress outside Congress offices for the unruly protest outside the PM's house yesterday," he said.Questioning Rahul Gandhi's approach, Prasad accused the Congress leader of abandoning dialogue and trying to dictate terms to the government."How do you intend to function? Will you just sit there forcibly? You were engaged in a dialogue. They were ready for a debate on the NEET issue, but then you backed out. Does this country run on your stick? Will it run on your arrogance? Rahul Gandhi, you have been irresponsible. I condemn your entire conduct," he said.Defending the police action during the protest, the BJP leader said security personnel had no option but to intervene to maintain law and order in the high-security zone."Later, the police were forced to take action, which was necessary for security and for maintaining peace. The Prime Minister has always been clear on these issues," Prasad said.Shifting focus to the controversy surrounding competitive examinations, Prasad asserted that the government had acted swiftly to protect the integrity of recruitment and entrance tests."In the past, irregularities were reported in several states during various examinations. Consequently, foolproof exams were conducted immediately after cancellations. The results have been declared with a 56-57% success rate, and students are satisfied. These exams were held without charging any additional fees," he told reporters.Emphasising the Centre's commitment to students, Prasad said those responsible for exam irregularities had been arrested and were facing trial."All the candidates appearing for NEET and other exams are our children. It is our duty to be concerned about their future, and we will fulfill that responsibility. Those involved in irregularities have been arrested and are facing trial. The government is ensuring that their trial leads to certain punishment," he said.The senior BJP leader concluded by reiterating Prime Minister Narendra Modi's assurance that the sanctity of NEET and other examinations would be protected through systemic reforms and stricter scrutiny.Meanwhile, another voice from the ruling BJP joined the attack on Rahul Gandhi. Senior BJP leader and MP Giriraj Singh told reporters, "Rahul Gandhi has tarnished the dignity of the Constitution while holding a constitutional position. His conduct is extremely dangerous. A case of sedition should be filed against Rahul Gandhi."The BJP's attack came a day after Rahul led the Opposition's march towards Lok Kalyan Marg, the official residence of the Prime Minister, where protesters came face-to-face with security personnel in the high-security Lutyens' Delhi zone.Videos from the scene showed police moving in to disperse the protesters gathered outside the Prime Minister's residence. In one video shared by the Congress on its official X handle, Rahul Gandhi was seen lying on the road as police personnel attempted to lift and remove him from the protest site. The former Congress president appeared to resist being taken away as security officials surrounded him.The Congress also released a photograph showing Rahul nosebleed following the police action, alleging excessive use of force during the protest.Rahul Gandhi's protest came amid Jantar Mantar protest demanding Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation over accountability in the NEET paper-leak.

World.title: 'Main bhi cockroach': Student protests against NEET reach New York, London - watch
World.content:
Protests spread to London

Protest continues

Cockroach Janata Party (CJP)

NEW DELHI: New York witnessed demonstrations in support of 'cockroaches', on Tuesday, as students and members of Indian diaspora rallied over alleged irregularities in the NEET examinations.The protesters gathered at the Mahatma Gandhi statue in New York City's Union Square carrying placards in support of students.Similar solidarity demonstrations were held in London, where protesters gathered outside the Indian High Commission in support of the nationwide movement demanding accountability over the alleged NEET irregularities and reforms in India's education system.Holding placards and raising slogans, the demonstrators expressed support and called for greater transparency, accountability and reforms in the country's examination and education system.Jantar Mantar continues to witness thousands of protesters on Wesneday days after the 'Sansad Chalo' march on July 20, as the agitation over alleged irregularities in the NEET examinations showed no signs of slowing down.On Tuesday, thecalled off its proposed sit-in outside the Delhi Police headquarters after claiming that all protesters detained following the march had been released. The outfit had earlier alleged that hundreds of its supporters were being held in custody and denied access to legal counsel, a charge that was rejected by the Delhi Police.Meanwhile, opposition parties have extended support to Wangchuk's agitation and staged protests in the national capital, demanding accountability over the alleged irregularities in the conduct of the NEET examination.

World.title: Daughter in SC, seeks return of Netaji's ashes from Japan
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Three months after a failed attempt by his grandnephew, Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose's octogenarian Germany-based daughter, Anita Pfaff, moved Supreme Court Tuesday seeking a direction to govt to bring his ashes back from the Renko-Ji temple in Japan.

Pfaff's petition, settled by senior advocate A M Singhvi, complained of "India's prolonged failure to take a final, reasoned and time-bound decision" to repatriate to India the "mortal remains/ashes attributed to Netaji, preserved at Renko-Ji temple" to allow the sole living direct lineal descendant to perform his last rites with dignity and finality.

"There is gross delay," said a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and Vipul M Pancholi.

However, it adjourned the hearing on Pfaff's petition on finding the arguing counsel absent.

Ahead of the West Bengal assembly elections, a petition was filed in SC by Netaji's gr-andnephew, Ashis Ray, seeking the same direction to the Centre. Appearing for Ray, Singhvi had argued before the bench of the same three judges on March 12 that the petition had the support of Pfaff, who joined the proceedings virtually.

Singhvi had said the fact that every head of state from India, over decades, had paid obeisance at Renko-Ji temple was proof that the freedom fighter's ashes were there.





The CJI-led bench had said there was no doubt that he was one of the country's greatest freedom fighters, but refused to entertain Ray's plea.

Justice Bagchi had said, "We respect her (Pfaff's) sentiments and we will ensure that her sentiments are translated into legal action. But she must step forward."

Singhvi had withdrawn the petition. Heeding SC's suggestion, Pfaff filed the petition seeking repatriation of Netaji's ashes by India or, as an alternative, "facilitate her to repatriate the ashes".

World.title: NEET protest: TVK slams govt; Rahul, Priyanka released from detention — top developments
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Congress leaders Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra were released after being detained by Delhi Police during a protest near Prime Minister Narendra Modi's residence.

The party had marched to Lok Kalyan Marg demanding the resignation of Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over the alleged paper leak and the police action against student protesters.

The protests also drew support from several opposition leaders, while Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) strongly criticised the Centre over Rahul Gandhi's detention and renewed its demand for the abolition of NEET.

Meanwhile, the BJP accused the Congress of politicising the issue and defended the police action, saying the protest near the Prime Minister's residence was held without permission.

The developments came as thousands of protesters returned to Jantar Mantar to continue the agitation.

FIR filed as video shows RAF jawan assaulted

Delhi Police registered an FIR after a Rapid Action Force (RAF) jawan was allegedly chased and assaulted by a group of protesters during the Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) "Sansad Chalo" march in New Delhi.





A video of the incident, widely shared on social media, appears to show the jawan being surrounded, pursued and beaten during Monday's protest. Police said an investigation is under way to identify those responsible.

TVK condemns Rahul's detention, seeks NEET abolition



Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK) condemned the detention of Rahul Gandhi and criticised the police action against opposition leaders.

"The crushing of democracy in the capital is strongly condemnable! The arrest of Lok Sabha Opposition Leader Mr.

Rahul Gandhi, who joined the field in support of the youth's non-violent protest held in Delhi, by being dragged by the Delhi Police and carried away in handcuffs, is a blatant attack on democratic rights. This is strongly condemnable," the party said.

TVK also renewed its opposition to the NEET examination.

"From the moment the NEET exam was implemented, not only has its credibility been lacking, but students continue to face mental stress, with their future dreams turning into a massive question mark.

The harm caused to students every year due to the NEET exam shows no sign of stopping. Therefore, we strongly demand that the Union government completely abolish the NEET exam," it said.

Rahul, Priyanka released after detention



Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi Vadra and several opposition leaders were detained after Congress workers marched towards the Prime Minister's residence at Lok Kalyan Marg.

Rahul Gandhi, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav and other leaders were taken to Chhatrasal Stadium before being released later in the day.

Priyanka Gandhi was taken to Mandir Marg Police Station, where Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi later arrived.

Congress leaders said they protested because they were not allowed to raise the NEET issue in Parliament. Rahul Gandhi said they marched to the Prime Minister's residence "to demand answers from him for the brutalities against young students yesterday" and demanded the resignation of the Prime Minister and the Home Minister.

The protest was joined by Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge, KC Venugopal, Pawan Khera, Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar, Kerala Leader of Opposition VD Satheesan, Supriya Sule and several other opposition leaders.

Pradhan hits out at Congress



Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan accused the Congress of using students for political purposes.

"LoP Shri @RahulGandhi and @INCIndia continue to shamelessly exploit students as political tools to manufacture disruption during the Monsoon Session of Parliament," he wrote on X.

He said the government was ready for a discussion on NEET in Parliament but alleged that the Congress preferred "political spectacle over democratic debate".

"We owe our students more than outrage. We owe them answers, reforms and accountability. That is exactly what our government remains committed to delivering," Pradhan said.

BJP MP Sambit Patra also criticised the protest, saying demonstrations should be held only at designated locations.

He said the Prime Minister's residence is a high-security zone and staging a protest there without permission was "inappropriate".

Police detail injuries, register six FIRs



Delhi Police said six FIRs have been registered in connection with the violence during Monday's Parliament march. Two FIRs were registered at Parliament Street police station, while one each was registered at Connaught Place, Tilak Marg, Barakhamba Road and Kartavya Path police stations.

DCP Northeast Delhi Rahul Alawal said six police personnel were injured during the violence. He said Constable Mohit suffered serious injuries to his head, below his eyes and on his legs and remains on medical rest. Additional DCP Sandeep Lamba, Inspector Rampal Goswami and some other officers have resumed duty despite being advised to rest.

Station House Officer of Connaught Place police station Sukhbir Singh Malik said he was assaulted when a section of protesters allegedly turned violent near Regal Cinema.

Malik said his helmet prevented a head injury, but he suffered injuries to his elbows, calf muscle and waist after being dragged to the ground. The police said several other personnel, including an ACP, an Inspector, a Head Constable and a driver, were also injured.

Sonam Wangchuk continues fast



Activist Sonam Wangchuk continued his indefinite hunger strike after being shifted from Safdarjung Hospital to Medanta Hospital in Gurugram following directions from the Delhi High Court.

Sources told news agency ANI said Union Health Minister JP Nadda and Minister of State in the Prime Minister's Office Jitendra Singh visited Medanta Hospital to enquire about Wangchuk's health.

The Delhi High Court directed Medanta Hospital to form a specialised medical team to supervise Wangchuk's treatment while allowing him to continue his fast under constant medical supervision. His wife, Gitanjali Angmo, said he would continue the hunger strike in solidarity with students allegedly injured during the police action.

World.title: Opposition using protest to find political relevance: BJP
World.content:
NEW DELHI:

had a go at opposition parties Tuesday as

attacked

over its dharna outside PM's residence on the NEET-UG paper leak issue, saying it is quite obvious that the "sponsored" protests were never about students but about the opposition's search for political relevance.

"It is quite obvious that the sponsored protests were never about students. No affected student was given a platform. Opposition politicians frequented Jantar Mantar in search of political relevance, and now, we see Congress and AAP squabbling over credit," BJP said as the Arvind Kejriwal-led party accused Congress of trying to weaken Cockroach Janta Party's protest.

Keeping up its attack over the protests, BJP alleged that all political assets of those resenting India's rise have been activated.

"But India's democracy is neither so fragile nor are the people of this country so naive that they cannot see their mandate being held to ransom by the sponsored outrage of a few," BJP's Amit Malviya said, adding the timing is no coincidence.

As India accelerates towards becoming a developed nation, every transformational initiative is met with a familiar cycle of disruption, disinformation and manufactured outrage, he claimed.





Malviya said at a time when the country is making rapid strides in different sectors, those who failed to stop India's rise electorally now seek to slow it through perpetual agitation, manufactured crises and a relentless campaign to erode public confidence.

World.title: 'Nadir of Indians' integrity': Allahabad HC judge slams Ram Mandir theft, backs death penalty
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Allahabad High Court judge, on Tuesday, made strong observations on the alleged embezzlement of donations at the Ram temple in Ayodhya, saying the incident reflected the"nadir of Indians' integrity"and that those unfazed by it could not be shamed.

The observations were made while the bench was hearing a matter related to the Uttar Pradesh government's recent bulldozer actions. During the hearing, Justice Sreedharan criticised the deep-rooted corruption in public institutions.

Backs death penalty

The judge also advocated the death penalty for offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act.

Justice Atul Sreedharan said, "The recent controversy relating to the theft of donations at the Ram temple is the proverbial last straw on the camel's back.

Nothing can shame people who remain unfazed by the theft at the Ram temple which epitomises the nadir of Indians' integrity"."

"The average Indian has accepted corruption as normal. He does not consider it wrong unless someone is caught. India ranks 91st out of 182 countries on the Transparency list, and even that does not make us feel ashamed," he added.

Supreme Court orders fresh SIT probe

The Supreme Court earlier has directed the constitution of a fresh Special Investigation Team (SIT) to probe the alleged Ram Mandir donation theft case.





A bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said the new SIT should be led by a senior IPS officer to ensure a fair and conclusive investigation.

"We only want to issue a word of caution. Do not politicise this matter. At first glance, this appears to be an offence under criminal law. It must be investigated fairly, independently and with complete honesty. The investigation should be taken to its logical conclusion," the CJI observed.

The case so far

The controversy erupted on June 7 after former Samajwadi Party minister Pawan Pandey alleged that donations worth Rs 5 crore to Rs 7.5 crore had been stolen from the Ram Mandir.

Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav questioned the government's silence and sought a judicial probe, while Ram Mandir Trust general secretary Champat Rai rejected the allegations. BJP leader Dr Rajneesh Singh later demanded a CBI investigation, following which the Prime Minister's Office sought a report from the temple trust.

An FIR was registered on June 25 on the complaint of trustee Krishna Mohan. Police has subsequently arrested eight accused in the matter till now.

World.title: 4 out of 10 healthcare workers worldwide face violence: WHO
World.content:
The incident took place at the Shastri Nagar Hospital, run by the Kalyan Dombivli Municipal Corporation (KDMC), in Kalyan on Monday evening.

MUMBAI: As the medical fraternity continues to press for stronger legal protection following Shiv Sena corporator Ramesh Mhatre's assault on doctors at Dombivli's Shastri Nagar Municipal Hospital, Indian Medical Association (IMA) Tuesday shared an interactive digital grid documenting 100 assaults on doctors reported from across the country in recent years.The campaign comes even as studies show that violence against healthcare workers by patients or their relatives has emerged as a global public health concern. A review published in the indexed medical journal, Atencion Primaria, found that doctors in both developed and developing countries face workplace violence. It reported lifetime prevalence rates of 91% in Germany, 90% in China, 84.5% in Peru, 84% in Turkey and 77.3% in India.According to WHO, four in 10 healthcare workers experience physical violence during their careers. When verbal abuse is included, the proportion rises to over 60%.The triggers for the attacks are universal, be it Mumbai or Singapore: overcrowded hospitals, staff shortages, long waiting times, poor communication and unrealistic patient expectations.Dr Santosh Kadam, former state IMA chief blames the attacks on impatience."We are becoming an impatient society. Everyone wants speedy results. People are spending money, so they want a 100% result," he said.Experts caution that ha-rsher laws alone are unlikely to solve the problem. They underline the need for a combination of measures, including greater investment in healthcare, stronger enforcement of laws, improved doctor-patient communication and awareness campaigns. Many Euro-pean countries observe Ma-rch 12 as a day to raise awareness about violence against healthcare professionals.In India, 19 states have enacted laws to protect healthcare workers, attacks continue. "What we need is one national law,'' said Dr Suhas Pingle, former Maharashtra Medical Council member.In Maharashtra, 738 cases were registered under Maharashtra Medicare Service Persons and Medicare Service Institutions (Prevention of Violence and Damage or Loss to Property) Act between 2010 and 2021, but only four ended in convictions.Spain strengthened legal protection by recognising assaults on healthcare workers as crimes against the state; assaults dropped by half. In Singapore, those who abuse healthcare workers can face a fine of up to S$5,000, jail for up to 12 months, or both.In India, Dr Kadam said, abuse is far more widespread than official records indicate. Dr Pingle said, "Medical practice has become tech-driven and expectations of patients are sky high. Barely 2% of the budget is meant for healthcare. Doctors have to see hundreds of patients in a short span of time. This creates an environment where the risk of violence is high," he said.

World.title: Bihar BJP delegation meets ECI, complains about Prashant Kishor’s expenditure in Bankipur byelection
World.content:
A delegation of the Bihar Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Tuesday (July 21, 2026) met Election Commission of India’s officials and submitted a memorandum against Jan Suraaj party leader Prashant Kishor concerning the Bankipur Assembly byelection.

The memorandum submitted by the BJP delegation raised concerns about the alleged violation of the prescribed election expenditure limit, spending funds through shell companies, and influencing voters through fake social media accounts and bot networks.

The delegation included Bihar Education Minister Mithilesh Tiwari, MLA Jivesh Mishra, Legislative Council Chief Whip Janak Ram, State Media In-charge Danish Iqbal, and Election Commission Cell Convener Rakesh Thakur.

Addressing a press conference at the BJP state office after meeting the ECI, senior party leader and former Union Minister Syed Shahnawaz Hussain said that while every individual has the right to contest elections in a democracy, adhering to the rules set by the Commission is mandatory for everyone.

He alleged that Mr. Kishor has spent crores of rupees in the Bankipur byelection, far exceeding the ₹40 lakh expenditure limit, and the BJP has provided documentary evidence to the ECI in this regard.

Mr. Hussain alleged that large-scale social media campaigning was being conducted through various companies to conceal actual election expenses. He added that payments are being made to influencers using fake social media accounts in an attempt to manufacture an artificial public sentiment.

The BJP leaders claimed that the election campaign was being conducted through companies such as Simple Sense Analytics Pvt. Ltd. and News Lighthouse LLP, which appear to be linked to Mr. Kishor. They demanded an impartial inquiry into the entire matter and urged the Enforcement Directorate (ED) to investigate the source of the funds.

Mr. Tiwari added that the BJP has submitted details to the Election Commission of India regarding several social media accounts that are based outside the country. He alleged that these foreign-operated accounts were being used to influence the political atmosphere in Bihar and to disseminate abusive language against political leaders. He urged that the Commission must take strict action in such cases to ensure the fairness of the election process.

Mr. Ram on the other hand, said that the people of Bankipur stand in support of development and good governance. He alleged that attempts were being made to spread misinformation through outsiders and social media, but the voters understood the truth.

The BJP leaders demanded that the Commission should conduct an impartial inquiry into the matter and take appropriate action regarding violations of the Model Code of Conduct (MCC) and the Representation of the People Act.

Reacting to the allegation, Jan Suraaj Party (JSP) Bihar State President Manoj Bharti told The Hindu that earlier the BJP never even considered that JSP was in a fight and they used to claim that the party had a direct fight with the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD).

“The anxiety and frustration among the BJP leaders prove that they too have admitted that their fight is with the JSP. We would also like to know what kind of proof they have submitted to the Commission in support of the allegation they have levelled against the JSP candidate. Basically, this act is childish; if at all they are raising questions on our funding, they should first disclose their funding. How much fund have they spent so far?” Mr. Bharati asked.

BJP has fielded Neeraj Kumar Sinha against Mr. Kishor, while RJD has fielded Rekha Kumari. Polling will be held on July 30, and counting of votes will take place on August 3.

District officials in multiple western U.P. districts on Tuesday (July 21, 2026) inspected security arrangements for the upcoming Kanwar Yatra. The Uttar Pradesh government has said it has pushed for zero incident, zero accident during the yatra.

The officials stressed the need for close coordination with neighbouring districts. “The administration and the police have almost completed their preparations for the Kanwar Yatra during the holy month of Shravan. Physical inspections have been carried out along the Bareilly route, Kachhla Ghat, and all other designated routes...” said Abhishek Kumar Singh, Additional Superintendent of Police (ASP) Budaun.

Similarly, physical inspections were carried out by police in Meerut, Saharanpur, Bijnor and Bareilly districts. Uttar Pradesh administration has established an Integrated Kanwar Control Room located at Police Lines, Meerut to ensure security, traffic management, and prompt and effective coordination between various departments along the Kanwar routes. The Chief Secretary, Government of Uttar Pradesh, and the Director General of Police, Uttar Pradesh, held a review meeting as well.

The Chief Secretary, Government of Uttar Pradesh, and the Director General of Police, Uttar Pradesh, have held multiple review meetings with the Additional Director General (ADG) police, Meerut Zone and other senior officers regarding preparations for yatra.

Earlier, U.P. Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath issued clear instructions that no negligence in security, cleanliness, or traffic management would be tolerated during the yatra. He directed officials to take immediate and strict action against anti-social elements spreading rumours on social media and to promptly counter misleading information.

“All concerned departments should complete their preparations before the commencement of the Kanwar Yatra. Adequate police personnel should be deployed along the entire yatra route. CCTV cameras should be installed at key locations, and continuous surveillance should be carried out through drones. Continuous coordination should be maintained during the Kanwar Yatra with officials of neighbouring states, including Delhi, Uttarakhand, Haryana, Punjab, and Rajasthan, so that any situation can be handled effectively,” said the U.P. CM.

World.title: Karnataka steps up drive to reduce trans fats in food supply chain; over 45 lakh litres of used cooking oil collected since 2024
World.content:
From roadside eateries to large food manufacturers, Karnataka is stepping up efforts to reduce the use of industrially-produced trans fats — a major contributor to heart disease and other non-communicable illnesses.

At a State-level sensitisation programme on eliminating industrially produced trans fats, held in Bengaluru on July 21, the Food Safety and Drug Administration (FSDA) Commissioner said Karnataka would intensify surveillance, inspection, and enforcement to ensure compliance with food safety regulations aimed at reducing trans fats in the food supply chain.

The programme brought together Food Safety Department officials, food business operators, edible oil manufacturers, industry representatives, and public health experts to discuss ways to strengthen implementation of the regulations.

Why trans fats matter

Officials pointed out that industrially produced trans fats, commonly found in partially hydrogenated oils used in some processed and fried foods, are among the most harmful dietary risk factors. Excess consumption has been linked to cardiovascular diseases, coronary heart disease, obesity, metabolic disorders, and adverse reproductive health outcomes.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), industrial trans fats are responsible for more than 278,000 deaths globally every year, including nearly 5,00,000 premature deaths from coronary heart disease. The WHO has called for their complete elimination from the global food supply chain.

India has adopted regulations limiting industrially produced trans fats to less than 2% in fats and oils, and Karnataka plans to strengthen compliance through enhanced surveillance, laboratory monitoring, risk-based inspections, and stricter enforcement across the food supply chain.

Focus on used cooking oil

The State has expanded awareness and capacity-building initiatives. More than 52,000 food business operators and professionals have been trained on safe food practices and trans-fat regulations.

Officials said the Repurpose Used Cooking Oil (RUCO) initiative has gained momentum, with 45.87 lakh litres of used cooking oil collected across Karnataka between 2024 and 2026. The initiative seeks to prevent repeated use of cooking oil by diverting used oil for industrial purposes, such as biodiesel production, instead of allowing it to re-enter the food chain.

Enforcement and awareness

Enforcement drives during the period resulted in penalties amounting to ₹28.91 lakh for violation of food safety norms. Awareness campaigns have been carried out through print, electronic and digital media.

The programme highlighted technical support from Vision for Social Development and Resolve to Save Lives in strengthening capacity building and evidence-based action on trans-fat elimination.

Officials said eliminating industrially produced trans fats would require sustained cooperation between regulators, the food industry and consumers, adding that Karnataka remained committed to creating a healthier food environment and reducing the burden of diet-related diseases.

World.title: Living by the sun, losing to the rain: life in Marakkanam’s salt pans in T.N.
World.content:
As Tamil Nadu swelters through one of its harshest summers in recent years, many look to the sky hoping for relief in the form of an afternoon shower. But in the salt pans of Marakkanam, rain is the one thing workers cannot afford to wish for. Every spell of rainfall stalls salt production for days and costs them wages.

So, even as they endure hours under a relentless sun that reflects off the white salt fields with blinding intensity, they hope for the heat to continue. It is a cruel irony that the weather which leaves workers dizzy, dehydrated, and exhausted is also what keeps their livelihoods alive.

This year, temperatures crossed the 40°C mark across several districts well into June, while high humidity made conditions feel even more oppressive. According to the Regional Meteorological Centre (RMC), the State recorded its second-highest average minimum temperature for June since 2015.

Nights remained nearly one degree Celsius warmer than normal, offering little relief to workers after a long day of manual labour. The lack of overnight cooling, coupled with prolonged daytime heat, left much of Tamil Nadu reeling under persistent heat stress. Even by mid-July, weak southwest monsoon conditions delayed widespread rainfall, extending heatwave-like conditions across many parts of the State.

Livelihoods from salt

Salt work is typically available from January to August in Tamil Nadu. Women earn between ₹400 and ₹500 a day, while men are paid ₹700 to ₹750. Workers usually begin around 6 a.m. and finish by 10 a.m., or until whenever the work is done, and come back around 3 p.m. when the volume of harvested salt is high.

Salt production follows a timed process that depends on dry weather. Seawater is channelled into evaporation pans and left to evaporate for several days until salt crystals form. The crystallised salt is then raked into piles, left to dry further, scraped into baskets and carried to large heaps, where it is covered with tarpaulin sheets until traders arrive to purchase it. Every change in the weather is closely watched, for even a brief drizzle can ruin an entire day’s harvest.

Navaneetham, 45, points to her legs, where the skin has darkened the skin, after years of working in the salt pans. “I always have boils on my feet,” she says.

She and her husband have taken a salt pan on sub-lease and do all the work themselves because they cannot afford to hire labourers. “We can’t pay anyone else, so we handle everything,” she says. The work is seasonal, which means the family has to manage without an income for nearly six months every year.

“We somehow survive by borrowing money. That’s how we’ve been eating,” she says. Their son, who completed a B.Com degree, briefly joined them in the salt pans but left for Chennai because he could not bear the heat.

Tamil Nadu provides a ₹5,000 annual monsoon relief assistance to registered salt pan workers to help sustain their families during the rainy months (October to December) when production halts. The aid is distributed to families registered under the Tamil Nadu Manual Workers Social Security and Welfare Board.

Since the assistance is provided on a per-family basis, only one member of the household is eligible to receive it. Although both Navaneetham and her husband are salt pan workers, the family received the State government’s ₹5,000 financial assistance for only one beneficiary.

Marakkanam is among Tamil Nadu’s traditional salt-producing regions, alongside major centres such as Thoothukudi, Vedaranyam and Cuddalore. However, unlike Thoothukudi, where large, contiguous salt fields enable large-scale production, Marakkanam’s salt pans are relatively smaller and more fragmented.

According to a salt pan manager, Thoothukudi remains the State’s largest salt-producing hub as the economies of scale keep production costs lower. “The pans there are much larger, so the cost of production is lower. The quality is also better. Buyers are willing to transport salt over longer distances because the overall cost still works out in their favour,” he says. As a result, traders often procure salt from Thoothukudi despite the higher transportation costs, making it a more competitive market compared to Marakkanam.

Climate change effects

The monsoon has always marked the end of the salt-making season, but, Sarasu, 50, a resident of Villivakkam in Marakkanam, says unseasonal summer showers are now eating into what was once a dependable period of work.

“It is becoming more and more precarious. Earlier, we could count on earning through most of the summer. Now, unseasonal rains cut the season short, and we somehow manage. The monsoon months are the hardest,” she said.

To get by, her family borrows small sums from neighbours, self-help groups and moneylenders, like most salt pan workers. With agricultural work becoming increasingly scarce during the off-season, her husband takes up whatever manual work he can find, often loading and unloading sacks for daily wages. But the earnings are irregular, and the loans accumulate. “We are trapped in a recurring cycle of debt. Because of this, I could not even get my children educated. They are doing odd jobs for survival now,” she says.

Burden on the body

As Selvalakshmi, 45, steps out of the salt pan after nearly four hours of work, she reaches for her neck. “... my neck hurts,” she exclaims with a weary smile. But there is no time to rest. She has to leave for her second job.

Widowed after her husband died of kidney disease, Selvalakshmi works two jobs to make ends meet. Once she finishes harvesting salt, she heads to a nearby cashew processing unit, where she removes the husk from cashew kernels. The work is paid on a piece-rate basis — ₹35 a kilogram.

“Yesterday, I managed to finish only five kilograms,” she says. “It’s difficult because I go there after finishing work here. By then, I’m already exhausted.”

Her husband, who had also worked in the salt pans, struggled with kidney disease before his death. In a 2023 study of seven Indian salt pans, published in Kidney International Reports, researchers from the Sri Ramachandra Institute of Higher Education and Research, led by Vidhya Venugopal, found that 87% of workers were exposed to unsafe levels of heat stress, while most consumed only about one litre of water during a workday. Many showed signs of dehydration and heat strain, and workers exposed to excessive heat were nearly three times more likely to have reduced kidney function.

More recently, a 2026 study by Prof. Venugopal published in Scientific Reports surveyed 1,560 outdoor workers across 11 districts in Tamil Nadu, including those employed in salt pans. The researchers found that workers exposed to higher levels of heat stress were 1.4 times more likely to report reduced productivity during summer, while their risk of heat-related illnesses — including dehydration, muscle cramps, headaches, nausea and fatigue — was more than twice as high.

An uncertain future

For Sudha, 35, the workday does not end when she steps out of the salt pan. It is only then that another concern begins: finding drinking water.

A resident of Pallampakkam village, she says there is no water because seawater intrusion has left the groundwater saline and unfit for drinking. “We’ve submitted petitions and even staged demonstrations, but we still don’t have drinking water,” she says. Residents depend largely on the neighbouring village for potable water.

Like most women working in the salt pans, Sudha starts her day with only tea and biscuits before heading to work. Aches have become part of the job. “Every part of the body hurts. It’s always there,” she says.

After work, some workers try to fill their bottles at a petrol bunk on the way home. But the shared autorickshaw that ferries them six to seven kilometres from their villages charges extra if it has to make the detour. Most instead rely on drinking water stored in cans at the salt pans by the lessee who manages the worksite, carrying home whatever they can.

In 2025, frequent summer showers brought the salt-making season to an abrupt end by June, nearly two months earlier than usual. Every rainy day means another day without work, which forces many families to borrow money to meet daily expenses. Workers say the State’s one-time financial assistance of ₹5,000 is nowhere near enough to sustain them through months without income.

Salt pan workers are among the communities most vulnerable to a changing climate. Their livelihoods depend on long spells of hot, dry weather for salt to crystallise, yet a single untimely shower can halt production for days. As rainfall patterns become increasingly erratic and extreme weather events more frequent, the financial precarity of salt pan workers is only expected to deepen, researchers say.

With few factories in and around Marakkanam, some women turn to agricultural labour during the off-season. But even that is uncertain. As Marakkanam is a town panchayat, they are ineligible for work under the Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme (MGNREGS), leaving them with few safety nets when the weather cuts short the salt season.

M. Krishnamoorthy, State vice president of the Unorganised Workers Federation, said the monsoon relief assistance should not be treated as charity and that the ₹5,000 support is inadequate to sustain workers through the off-season.

“Salt is fundamental to everyday life. It is in every meal we eat and is used across industries. The workers who produce it deserve far better compensation,” he said, adding that the board should be made operational by levying a cess on salt traders to generate funds for the welfare of salt workers.

He further said that although the State had announced a dedicated welfare board for salt workers, it had failed to address the challenges faced by the community.

An official in the Labour Department said the Tamil Nadu Salt Workers Welfare Board, announced in 2023, remains largely non-functional as the department is working out how it can be operationalised under the new labour codes.

(This story is part of the Asian College of Journalism’s Climate Change Media Hub Mentorship Programme.)
