World.title: Sidebottom set to exit, one of Pendlebury and Howe makes sense
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 Sidebottom set to exit, one of Pendlebury and Howe makes sense Jake Niall July 22, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Soon, before the season’s close, Collingwood are expected to announce that their two-time premiership great Steele Sidebottom will retire. For several weeks, the signs have pointed to Sidebottom finishing at Collingwood this year. After a stellar first half of 2025, when he was close to All-Australian standard, there has been a gradual ebbing of performances on the field for the distinguished 35-year-old. Big decisions: Collingwood need to manage the eventual exits of club greats Steele Sidebottom and Scott Pendlebury. Getty Images Sidebottom is said to be comfortable with the prospect of finishing his career, which will fall shy of the 400-game mark (370 now), according to sources familiar with his situation. The positions of Scott Pendlebury – the AFL’s games record holder and one of Collingwood’s immortals – and the remarkable veteran aerialist Jeremy Howe are yet to settled on by the players or the Magpies as August beckons.



But the most logical scenario is that only one of Pendlebury or Howe will play on at Collingwood in 2027. It’s even conceivable that neither does. It is open to either of Pendlebury or Howe to either retire or seek to finish their playing days at another club and then (assistant) coach there, as Sam Mitchell did at West Coast in 2017-18. Both have an interest in coaching. Lachie Neale is heavily linked to a Magpies move in the off-season. AFL Photos Collingwood recently had a follow-up meeting with Brisbane Lions champion Lachie Neale. That the parties have met more than once can be read as confirmation that the Magpies are genuine frontrunners for the dual Brownlow medallist; they have gone beyond the first date. To gain Neale means that a midfield spot must be open. The uncertainty around who is coming (Neale, and the longshot of Port Adelaide’s Zak Butters), and who’s retiring is an explanation for Collingwood’s reticence in offering the improved Ed Allan a contract, even though their preference is to retain Allan.



Collingwood’s need to regenerate their list, while remaining in finals contention, means that the exits of veterans has to continue to be staggered. Jamie Elliott, whose knee injury on Pendlebury’s record-breaking day ended his season, is contracted for 2027. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Try before you buy: Why Fraser’s no-strings audition suits him and the Blues To borrow from Meat Loaf (who performed far worse than any Collingwood player on 2011 grand final day), two out of three (retiring) ain’t bad. To transition the list and provide opportunities for younger players, the Magpies ideally would keep no more than one of their trio of super veterans, who are 38, 36 (Howe) and 35. Howe might hold appeal to rival clubs if Collingwood do not wish to continue with him. Until his record-breaker against West Coast, Pendlebury was playing well and often enough for both he and Collingwood to continue their 21-year marriage in 2027.



Early this season, he was even rated inside the top-20 performing AFL players by Champion Data; since then, there’s been some niggles and a dip. Always quicker of mind than legs, Pendlebury seems to have slowed further lately, albeit his vision and smarts remain exceptional. If he is adamant about playing on, the Magpies would find it difficult to stop him. It’s not easy to diss a statue. But Pendlebury’s last comment on his future was that he was undecided. “I’m not sure,” he told Seven. “I’m enjoying my footy and taking it day by day.” In terms of holes and roles at Collingwood, Howe shapes as the one whom the Magpies might need most. They do not have an abundance of tall backs, and with Darcy Moore sidelined, Howe – who retains much of his spring – would afford a level of protection for a backline that has sometimes been compelled to play Brayden Maynard on tall opponents.



Rory Sloane opined on Nine last week that Howe would be an ideal recruit for Essendon, as a veteran and educator of a young backline. One could argue the same of Richmond, who will lose Nathan Broad to West Coast or Gold Coast. View post on X Had Tasmania been entering the AFL a year earlier than 2028, Howe, as a Tassie man, would surely have been in their sights as a foundation leader who’d join their coaching panel after one or two years playing. Howe, slated to return for this Thursday night’s game in Adelaide, will have options, as will Pendlebury. For the latter, his stature as club and AFL legend is a significant incentive to remain a one-clubber. The Sherrin is in Collingwood’s court, as much as theirs. World.title: Shopkeeper survives leopard attack by a whisker
World.content:
WorldAsiaAnimal attacks Shopkeeper survives leopard attack by a whisker Lily Shanagher July 22, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A leopard lunged at men after bursting into a shop selling alcohol in India. Security camera footage of the store in Todaraisingh, Rajasthan, captured the animal leaping over the counter and pouncing on Sanjay Gurjar, 25. Loading The shopkeeper managed to shake off the leopard, which launched itself twice at him and grabbed his back, attempting to bite him, before he managed to run off, locking the animal inside. The big cat was then seen prowling around the empty shop, knocking over boxes before hiding under a shelf.



Related Article India Elusive big cats and humans live side by side in this alien-like landscape A second piece of footage taken in the storeroom shows the leopard lunging at a different man, Fateh Lal Koli, 40, knocking him across the room and to the floor before it dashes over the shelf and after Gurjar. Gurjar suffered claw injuries to his hand, shoulder and nose, while two other men also sustained injuries. The leopard had attacked a forest ranger volunteer on Sunday morning, officials told Indian media. The ranger had been investigating reports the leopard had been seen in bushes at 8.45am (Indian time) when the animal attacked him.



The animal then travelled into the northern town, where it entered the alcohol shop and attacked its second and third victims. A rescue team reached the town about 2pm and launched a five-hour operation to track and capture the leopard. Police cleared a cordon around the shop and shut the main market before calling in a specialist animal rescue unit. Officials said the leopard was a five-year-old male that will be given medical checks before being returned to the wild. Virender Singh Krishniya, deputy conservator of forests, said the animal was believed to have strayed into the town in search of prey after leaving surrounding forests. World.title: New York’s Mamdani says the city can’t arrest Netanyahu for war crimes
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's America New York’s Mamdani says the city can’t arrest Netanyahu for war crimes Liam Stack July 22, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Mayor Zohran Mamdani has challenged the federal government to execute an international arrest warrant against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, calling him a “war criminal” and “the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people” in a striking video statement. The mayor said the city’s law department explored whether the New York Police Department could arrest the Israeli prime minister during his expected visit to the city in September, but that the city did not have “independent legal authority” to do so. Loading The mayor’s announcement came days after he said in an interview with The New York Times Magazine that he had been in “active conversation” with the city’s law department about executing a warrant issued for Netanyahu in 2024 by the International Criminal Court. US President Donald Trump has ruled out any chance of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu being arrested. Getty Images



On Tuesday (US time), Mamdani said in the video that those conversations had led his administration to determine it does “not have the independent legal authority to enforce this warrant.” Related Article Analysis

US politics The kingmaker who stunned the US Democratic establishment – again Seated between the flags of the United States and New York City, Mamdani looked directly into the camera and solemnly told New Yorkers that Israel’s prime minister had no place visiting the city. “Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City, nor is any other war criminal at large,” Mamdani said. “While we cannot end the genocide on our own, we can decide whether our silence will become another weapon, and we can examine every tool we have to defend the humanity and dignity of all people.”



There appears to be no chance of federal law enforcement arresting Netanyahu in the near future. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the Israeli leader, whose country is a longtime US ally, would not be arrested in the United States “in any way, shape, or form”. The US is not a member of the International Criminal Court, which blunts the impact of the court’s warrant. On Tuesday night, Israel’s UN ambassador Danny Danon criticised Mamdani’s video in a statement posted online. “Enough with the blood libels,” Danon said. “You were elected to serve New Yorkers, not Hamas’ propaganda. Do your job!” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he had been in “active conversation” with the New York City Law Department about executing a warrant issued for Netanyahu in 2024 by the International Criminal Court. AP Photo/Seth Wenig



Mamdani had said during his mayoral campaign that he would order the Police Department to arrest Netanyahu if he were to visit New York, as the prime minister is expected to do in September for the United Nations General Assembly. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict The numbers that show what two years of war have done to Palestinian lives But the legal ability of the mayor to order such a move has long been in doubt. After he discussed the possibility with the Times last week, Mamdani was denounced by Netanyahu’s office, which said he “should focus on fixing the damage his policies have caused New York.” “Mamdani appears interested in diverting public attention from his follies and attacking the leader of the Jewish state and the only democracy in the Middle East,” the prime minister’s office said in a statement on Sunday. The mayor was also denounced on Monday by Danon, who said in an address to the General Assembly that there was “no legal basis” for Mamdani to order the arrest of Netanyahu. Danon accused him of engaging in “political theatre” to energise his “radical base.”



View post on X The international court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant, in 2024 on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip, where more than 70,000 people have been killed in a war that began after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, terrorist attack on Israel. The ICC warrants accused both Netanyahu and Gallant of having “intentionally and knowingly deprived” the population of Gaza of food, water, fuel and medicine, which both Netanyahu and Gallant have denied. The court also issued an arrest warrant for Hamas’ military chief, Muhammad Deif, for crimes against humanity, but Israel said it had killed Deif in an airstrike before the warrant could be issued. Israel’s conduct during the war in Gaza has been described as genocide by Israeli and international human rights groups, as well as by two separate UN commissions, one of which issued its findings last month.



Related Article Analysis

Middle East at war Trump claims he calls ‘all the shots’. Netanyahu and Iran have other ideas Israel has rejected those findings, and Netanyahu’s office said Sunday that “Israel has taken unprecedented wartime measures to minimise harm to civilians while confronting Hamas.” But Israel’s actions in Gaza have left it deeply isolated on the global stage and increasingly unpopular in the United States, its most important ally. According to the Pew Research Centre, polls show that a majority of Americans now hold a negative view of Israel, including majorities of adults under age 50 in both political parties. Among Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents, that number rises to 80 per cent.



This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: As net closed in after 30 years, accused Chadstone shooter said he better ‘take the medicine’, court hears
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts As net closed in after 30 years, accused Chadstone shooter said he better ‘take the medicine’, court hears Erin Pearson July 22, 2026 — 3:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A great-grandfather and former rugby league player was allegedly tied to a violent Armaguard hold-up at Chadstone Shopping Centre after 30 years by DNA on a glove left at the scene by the gunman. As the net closed on Garry Sullivan, 78, he was captured on a listening device telling his wife it was time to “take the medicine”, a court has heard. Garry Sullivan during his extradition to Victoria. Nine News Sullivan was arrested in Queensland in May and extradited to Victoria after detectives reopened the 1994 case that left three people with gunshot wounds and $80,000 in cash missing. Melbourne Magistrates’ Court was told on Wednesday that Sullivan had escaped jail and was on the run when he allegedly used a pistol to hold up two Armaguard employees on May 16, 1994.



The court heard Sullivan allegedly shot one officer in the ankle, with the bullet ricocheting off him and through the right foot of a second guard. A third person, a bystander, was shot in the thigh as they attempted to follow the shooter to get his vehicle registration. The court heard that in the lead-up to the Chadstone incident, Sullivan and his stepfather had netted more than $3.2 million from robberies committed in the ’80s and ’90s, and were jailed for 20 years. The scene where two security guards were shot in May 1994 after being ambushed beside their Armaguard truck in a daylight heist that spilled into the busy Chadstone shopping centre. Nine News But Sullivan, the court heard, had cut a hole in a wire fence at the prison and escaped. During his time on the run he allegedly travelled to Chadstone. Sullivan was eventually rearrested in South Australia and locked up until 2005. He had been living in the community ever since, the prosecution said.



But court documents allege he was doing so with unexplained wealth. Sullivan is also charged with dealing in the proceeds of crime, about $366,000 police allege was laundered through his Tabcorp betting account between February 2020 and May 2026. Sullivan in his playing days. Of the money, $218,000 was withdrawn as Sullivan gambled prolifically while living in housing commission accommodation and on the pension. The court heard that when police reopened the Chadstone case, they compared a DNA sample of Sullivan that was on file with the glove from the scene, and it was “a billion to one” match. They then laid “bait” and captured him on listening devices correctly identifying to his wife the type of lead used to shoot the guards, the court was told.



“I’m just going to sit here and wait for them to come,” he allegedly told her. “I better take the medicine. You know what I mean.” Sverre Benjaminsen, one of two security guards shot on May 16, 1994. Nine News Sullivan applied to be freed on bail, which the prosecution opposed, comparing the man with ailing health to police killer Dezi Freeman, fearing he too could escape police apprehension once more. “It’s not that hard for somebody to abscond and if one has the means to do so, and there’s enough at stake,” prosecutor Francesca Holmes said.



Defence lawyer Matthew Cramer said his client was a father of four and grandfather of nine, a reformed family man who posed no risk of flight. His daughter, Kim Robertson, said her father had lived with his partner, Heather, for 49 years and had coeliac disease, pointing to a fall and 12-kilogram weight loss since his arrest. “He’s a regular granddad, he’s a regular dad to us,” she said. The court heard Sullivan had mouth cancer and heart disease, and his age added to his vulnerability in custody. Any alleged risk of flight was fanciful, Cramer said, with Sullivan having lived countless lives, including as a rugby league star, in the ’60s and ’70s, before his criminal notoriety began.



“We’re not Dezi Freeman,” Cramer said. “He’s now a dedicated family man.” Magistrate Patrick Southey agreed that Sullivan’s dedicated career as an armed robber in the ’80s and ’90 was “last millennium” and his fall from grace decades ago. He reminded those in the court of the presumption of innocence but maintained exceptional circumstances had not been established and refused bail. Sullivan is expected to return to court in October. World.title: Peak Jewish group says Labor platform ‘regurgitates one-eyed obsession with Israel’
World.content:
The head of the nation’s peak Jewish body has condemned Labor for removing a call for listed terror group Hamas to disarm from its draft policy platform despite Prime Minister Anthony Albanese making the stance a core plank of his Middle East policy. Labor planned to present a unified front on the contentious issue by having two Labor MPs from Melbourne – Josh Burns, who is Jewish, and Bassem Abdo, the son of Palestinian refugees – jointly present the section of the platform on Israel/Palestine in Adelaide on Saturday, the last day of the party’s national conference. Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Peter Wertheim said he was disappointed by the wording of the draft platform. Dominic Lorrimer But infighting over wording of the manifesto, which was recently amended to be tougher on Israel and less demanding of the Palestinian side, threatens to derail hopes for an uplifting moment. Executive Council of Australian Jewry co-chief executive Peter Wertheim, a longtime confidant of Albanese, said the draft platform lacked balance and failed to reflect the government’s stated policy positions.



“Instead of providing an honest assessment of the leadership on both sides of the conflict, the draft platform regurgitates the same old one-eyed obsession with blaming Israel,” Wertheim said in the Jewish peak body’s first comments on the draft platform. Related Article ALP Israel accused of ‘extraordinary’ intervention in Labor politics “It is a reasonable question to ask why the ALP national conference is not backing in the Albanese government in expressly recognising the government’s position on excluding Hamas and requiring the Palestinian Authority to honour the commitments for governance reform upon which the government’s recognition of a Palestinian state was explicitly based.” Wertheim said Albanese and Foreign Minister Penny Wong had repeatedly argued there must be no role for Hamas in Gaza, raising questions about why wording reflecting this stance had been expunged from the draft platform. “Even Hamas itself has acknowledged it, by announcing a hand-over of its government functions to a US-backed technocratic committee,” Wertheim told this masthead.



“But apparently the ALP National Conference cannot quite bring itself to acknowledge it. The best it can do is refer to Hamas, in passing, as a terrorist group.” Wertheim said the platform also failed to reflect the government’s insistence that recognition of Palestinian statehood relied on commitments from the Palestinian Authority, which governs parts of the West Bank, to reform its governance, terminate payments to the families of Palestinian prisoners, institute schooling reform, and hold general elections. “The draft platform says nothing about any of this, or the fact that there has not been the slightest progress towards fulfilling the commitments made by the Palestinian Authority to the Australian government,” he said. Wertheim and Albanese formed a bond two decades ago when Albanese opposed the boycott, divestment and sanctions movement against Israel, and Albanese regularly consults Wertheim on matters related to the Jewish community. Albanese told the United Nations General Assembly last September that “the terrorist organisation Hamas can have no role in Palestine’s future”, adding Australia’s recognition of a Palestinian state was predicated on a set of commitments from the Palestinian Authority, including that “Hamas would hand over its weapons to Palestinian security forces – and never control Gaza again”.



Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict Israel blasts Labor’s ‘one-sided’ policy platform as Palestinian advocates push further When announcing $25 million in new aid funding for Palestine on Tuesday, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said: “This package demonstrates Australia’s practical commitment to Palestinian recovery, reform and institution-building. Hamas can play no role in the State of Palestine.” Several Labor sources said former cabinet minister Ed Husic, a fierce critic of Israel’s conduct in the war in Gaza, had been pushing internally for the platform to go further in its criticisms of Israel. Husic did not respond to requests for comment. The latest version of the draft platform condemns the use of violence, including by Hamas, but earlier versions included an explicit reference that “Hamas must disarm and can have no role in the State of Palestine”.



An earlier draft also said that Labor “will continue to work with the international community to hold the Palestinian Authority to its commitments and to encourage normalised relations between Israel and its neighbours”. This wording was also removed from the latest version. The draft version calls out Israel for settler violence in the West Bank, condemns a controversial new death penalty law and backs two international courts considering genocide and war crimes charges against Israel. The Israeli embassy in Canberra said in a lengthy statement issued on Monday that it “respectfully submits that several elements of the draft national platform risk placing responsibility for the conflict on one party while giving insufficient attention to the decisions, conduct and continuing obligations of the Palestinian leadership and terrorist organisations such as Hamas”. The Palestinian delegation in Canberra welcomed the draft platform and called for the government to go further by giving practical effect to last year’s decision to recognise Palestinian statehood. World.title: Safety tightened after Sea World helicopter tragedy
World.content:
NationalQueenslandTragedy Safety tightened after Sea World helicopter tragedy Robyn Wuth July 22, 2026 — 3:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Tourist helicopter joyrides outside one of Australia’s biggest theme parks have undergone a safety overhaul since a mid‑air crash killed four people. Three tourists and Sea World Helicopters pilot Ashley Jenkinson were killed in a mid-air collision between two helicopters near the Gold Coast theme park on January 2, 2023. Current chief pilot and head of operations Ben Hall – a long‑time colleague and friend of Jenkinson – said the company now operating as Surfers Paradise Helicopters had brought in a suite of new controls aimed at preventing another collision in the busy Broadwater airspace. The Sea World helicopters in the aftermath of the crash. AAP The firm now records radio calls from its operations to ensure pilots are broadcasting at the right times and positions, Hall told the Queensland Coroners Court on Wednesday.



The real-life recordings were used as a training and surveillance tool during flight reviews or proficiency checks with pilots, he said. The company had also adopted “sterile cockpit” procedures, requiring passengers to remain quiet during take‑off and landing so flight crews can focus on checklists and radio calls. Ashley Jenkinson, the pilot who died in the Gold Coast helicopter crash. Facebook Pilots must now ensure sterile cockpit conditions below 500 feet (150 metres) on departure and approach to reduce potential distractions. The inquest heard the joyflight company also formalised and expanded the role of a “pad boss” on the helipad, with specially trained staff using two radios – a UHF set to speak directly with pilots and a VHF handheld to monitor calls across the general aviation frequency.



Pad bosses are trained to listen for key taxi and airborne broadcasts and to radio pilots if expected calls are missed, while scanning for other hazards such as boats, birds and other aircraft near the pads. Sea World Helicopters was running about 7500 flights a year at the time of the crash, but that number had since fallen, the inquest heard. “It’s a demand‑based business,” Hall said. “If tourism increased on the Gold Coast, then our flight numbers would increase.” Hall, who had known Jenkinson since about 2008, said the pair worked together as line pilots in central Australia and later crossed paths in Melbourne and on the Gold Coast, socialising at parties and dinners over many years.



He described Jenkinson as “a very likeable fella” who was kind, polite and professional, saying nothing in their friendship had suggested an interest in illicit drugs. Related Article Inquest Onus on pilots to ‘keep head on a swivel’ in busy skies around Sea World crash site Hall told the court he was shocked to learn of evidence that Jenkinson had taken cocaine in the lead‑up to the fatal flight. “We spent a lot of time socialising and attending parties, social events together, restaurant dinners,” he said. “Throughout that whole time, there was never any discussion or talk about any drugs.”



Hall became chief pilot in August 2023, months after the crash, in his first chief pilot role. The inquest previously heard pilots describe the Gold Coast Broadwater as a busy, unforgiving environment where they had to “keep their head on a swivel” and rely on looking out the window to avoid conflict, with multiple helicopters operating from closely spaced pads near the theme park. But the aviation safety authority’s air navigation boss, Adrian Slootjes, told the inquest a formal, data‑driven review found the Gold Coast airspace was appropriately controlled and operating safely, with no present need for a manned control tower. “Nothing eliminates risk – nothing that we do here eliminates risk,” Mr Slootjes said. Sea World owner Village Roadshow Theme Parks sold its joy flights operation to Sea World Helicopters in 2019. The firm dumped the Sea World name on July 1.



The inquest continues. AAP Get alerts on significant breaking news as happens.

World.title: ‘Transformative’: Green light for $240m Perth CBD revamp with hotel and rooftop pool
World.content:
NationalWACity life ‘Transformative’: Green light for $240m Perth CBD revamp with hotel and rooftop pool Indigo Lemay-Conway July 22, 2026 — 3:41pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A $240 million megaproject is set to breathe new life into the iconic St Martins Centre, officially securing the green light for a makeover into a 240-room hotel with a retail hub and office spaces. The Metro Inner Development Assessment Panel unanimously approved the plans on Wednesday morning, of which also included the redevelopment of the heritage-listed McNess Royal Arcade and Bridal House. An aerial view of what the St Martins Centre development could look like. Metro Inner Development Assessment Panel St Martins Properties owns three consecutive office towers on St Georges Terrace, with the hotel set to be built at number 44. The rotating restaurant at level 33 is intended to be retained and repurposed as a “sky bar facility” with additional supporting amenities for the new hotels to be built on levels two and three.



A new three-storey building will be added on the back that will host dining, retail and wellness functions as well as a podium rooftop-level pool club. The new development will also feature a podium rooftop level pool club. Metro Inner Development Assessment Panel Primary office use will be retained at 40 and 50 St Georges Terrace, but with a new ground floor retail and dining area introduced to activate St Georges Terrace and Barrack Street. McNess Royal Arcade was Perth’s first city shopping mall and was built in 1897. The new development works are anticipated to be completed within four years across various stages.



Project proponent Daniel Lees from SLR Consulting said the building addition would be a game changer for the area. “St Martin’s Centre, which comprises three office towers and extensive frontage to Hay Street Mall, is one of the most recognisable commercial precincts in Central Perth,” he said. An artist Impression of the reinstated McNess Royal Arcade. Metro Inner Development Assessment Panel “This project will breathe new life into the locality, complementing the surrounding sites and the success of adjacent precincts like the Treasury, and presents an opportunity for the retention and future adaptive reuse of the heritage-listed McNess Royal Arcade and Bridal House buildings.” Lees said the hotel addition as well as more contemporary food, beverage and entertainment offerings will help to expand the hours of activation of the nearby streets beyond the current 9am to 5pm focus.



City of Perth councillor Liam Gobbert said he was glad to see St Martins Properties factoring in the heritage aspect into their proposal. “I’m very happy to support the recommendation and hopefully the four-year time frame proposed as part of the application doesn’t take that long,” he said. An artist impression of the $240 million development at St Martins Centre. Metro Inner Development Assessment Panel Panel presiding member Dale Page said she was “very pleased” with the plans for the multimillion dollar proposal. “This is a very prominent and important site within the heart of the city, and has frontage to three of its most prominent pedestrian thoroughfares and focal points,” she said.



“I’m especially pleased to see some adaptive reuse of the upper floors of heritage listed buildings, which have been a challenge in this area of the city in the past. “I just hope that, given they’re currently planned as the last stage of works, that they are progressed and sooner rather than later.”

World.title: The Odyssey has called it: Guilt is good
World.content:
CultureMoviesPodcasts The Odyssey has called it: Guilt is good Samantha Selinger-Morris July 22, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

It’s not every day that a 2700-year-old Greek poem causes people to lose their ever-loving minds. But the release of Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster The Odyssey - a retelling of Homer’s epic poem - has unleashed all sorts of anger. Elon Musk called Nolan – for his decision to cast the award-winning Kenyan actress, Lupita Nyong’o, as Helen of Troy, an “anti-white racist” guilty of “pissing on Homer’s grave”. Christopher Nolan, who wrote, directed and produced The Odyssey, on set. Melinda Sue Gordon Others have taken the famed director to task for minimising the role of the goddesses in the original story. (“You have adapted one of the strangest, wildest, most sexually complicated, most glorious irrational poems ever written into a support group for emotionally unavailable men,” read one take on social media.) You know who’s not bothered?



Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy in The Odyssey. Universal Pictures One of the United States’ most revered classicists is Daniel Mendelsohn, a professor at Bard College. He recently spent six years translating The Odyssey, line for line. (It was published last year.) And, as he wrote on X two days ago, he thinks lovers of literature, Homer, and The Odyssey should be “rejoicing” at the release of this film. “If you’d told me five years ago that the entire planet would be talking about this 2,700-year-old Greek text, I’d have laughed,” he wrote. “So let’s be grateful.” For one thing, he says artists over time have refashioned Odysseus to suit their own purpose. So, what did he think of Nolan’s celluloid refashioning? And what might it have to teach us? Matt Damon as Odysseus and Zendaya as Athena in The Odyssey.



To find out, I interviewed him on The Morning Edition. In today’s episode of The Morning Edition podcast, host Samantha Selinger-Morris talks to The New York Review of Books editor-at-large Daniel Mendelsohn. The classics scholar discusses what Nolan is trying to tell us, and why it has provoked such a visceral reaction. Samantha Selinger-Morris: You have written that over many years, other poets have taken Odysseus and sort of refashioned him for their own purposes. In Dante’s Inferno, Odysseus, who’s called Ulysses, is damned for deceitfulness and madly sails over the edge of the world. And then you’ve written that in the 19th century, Odysseus’s perpetual restlessness made him a romantic hero. So, what do you think of how Christopher Nolan has refashioned his hero? And what does it tell us about the time that we’re living in, perhaps something that Christopher Nolan thinks we need to hear or be reminded of? Daniel Mendelsohn: Well, certainly. I mean, The Odyssey has made this character available to subsequent generations. And so, Nolan – I’m a big Nolan fan – I have admired a lot of his movies. And what he has done is he has taken the hero of the Odyssey, who is a trickster, there’s something very charming and almost, dare I say, James Bond-ish about Odysseus. Well, he’s a seducer, he’s a warrior, he’s a trickster, you know, and that’s sort of why we like him... And what Nolan has done in this film is to turn our charming, clever, seductive, amusing, James Bond-ish Odysseus into a guilt-ridden hero. So, the sort of operative theme of the movie is that he’s tormented by guilt, about having won the Trojan War and the terrible destruction of Troy that followed the Greek victory.



Selinger-Morris: Do you think that message is particularly resonant, perhaps, in this geopolitical climate? Mendelsohn: Well, remember, guilt is a modern notion. The Greeks didn’t experience guilt; they experienced what anthropologists – they were what anthropologists call a shame culture. So, you acted in a certain way because you didn’t want to be shamed by other people in your group, not because you felt an internal sense of guilt, but because this shame was being imposed from outside. So, it’s not a very Greek notion. But I do think your point is very well taken. Certainly, this kind of guilt-ridden character is a kind of character we’re familiar with... This is about one guy trying to make his [way] home through a kind of post-apocalyptic landscape where he doesn’t know the rules anymore... And for that reason, I feel it’s very modern. Selinger-Morris: Is that particularly resonant in the Donald Trump era, do you think? Mendelsohn: Yeah... there is... I always say there’s something kind of “post” about the Odyssey, if that makes sense. We’re in... we’re in new territory, and we haven’t yet figured it out. And in that sense, I do think it speaks to modern times. We’re post... God knows, we’re post everything. The old order, certainly the global geopolitical order, is falling apart. And so I do think we identify with this sense that you get in the Odyssey of this guy who doesn’t know what the rules are, he’s just making it up as he goes along, and that feels very modern, I think.

World.title: Sidebottom set to exit, one of Pendlebury and Howe makes sense
World.content:
Analysis SportAFLAFL 2026 Sidebottom set to exit, one of Pendlebury and Howe makes sense Jake Niall July 22, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Soon, before the season’s close, Collingwood are expected to announce that their two-time premiership great Steele Sidebottom will retire. For several weeks, the signs have pointed to Sidebottom finishing at Collingwood this year. After a stellar first half of 2025, when he was close to All-Australian standard, there has been a gradual ebbing of performances on the field for the distinguished 35-year-old. Big decisions: Collingwood need to manage the eventual exits of club greats Steele Sidebottom and Scott Pendlebury. Getty Images Sidebottom is said to be comfortable with the prospect of finishing his career, which will fall shy of the 400-game mark (370 now), according to sources familiar with his situation. The positions of Scott Pendlebury – the AFL’s games record holder and one of Collingwood’s immortals – and the remarkable veteran aerialist Jeremy Howe are yet to settled on by the players or the Magpies as August beckons.



But the most logical scenario is that only one of Pendlebury or Howe will play on at Collingwood in 2027. It’s even conceivable that neither does. It is open to either of Pendlebury or Howe to either retire or seek to finish their playing days at another club and then (assistant) coach there, as Sam Mitchell did at West Coast in 2017-18. Both have an interest in coaching. Lachie Neale is heavily linked to a Magpies move in the off-season. AFL Photos Collingwood recently had a follow-up meeting with Brisbane Lions champion Lachie Neale. That the parties have met more than once can be read as confirmation that the Magpies are genuine frontrunners for the dual Brownlow medallist; they have gone beyond the first date. To gain Neale means that a midfield spot must be open. The uncertainty around who is coming (Neale, and the longshot of Port Adelaide’s Zak Butters), and who’s retiring is an explanation for Collingwood’s reticence in offering the improved Ed Allan a contract, even though their preference is to retain Allan.



Collingwood’s need to regenerate their list, while remaining in finals contention, means that the exits of veterans has to continue to be staggered. Jamie Elliott, whose knee injury on Pendlebury’s record-breaking day ended his season, is contracted for 2027. Related Article Analysis

AFL 2026 Try before you buy: Why Fraser’s no-strings audition suits him and the Blues To borrow from Meat Loaf (who performed far worse than any Collingwood player on 2011 grand final day), two out of three (retiring) ain’t bad. To transition the list and provide opportunities for younger players, the Magpies ideally would keep no more than one of their trio of super veterans, who are 38, 36 (Howe) and 35. Howe might hold appeal to rival clubs if Collingwood do not wish to continue with him. Until his record-breaker against West Coast, Pendlebury was playing well and often enough for both he and Collingwood to continue their 21-year marriage in 2027.



Early this season, he was even rated inside the top-20 performing AFL players by Champion Data; since then, there’s been some niggles and a dip. Always quicker of mind than legs, Pendlebury seems to have slowed further lately, albeit his vision and smarts remain exceptional. If he is adamant about playing on, the Magpies would find it difficult to stop him. It’s not easy to diss a statue. But Pendlebury’s last comment on his future was that he was undecided. “I’m not sure,” he told Seven. “I’m enjoying my footy and taking it day by day.” In terms of holes and roles at Collingwood, Howe shapes as the one whom the Magpies might need most. They do not have an abundance of tall backs, and with Darcy Moore sidelined, Howe – who retains much of his spring – would afford a level of protection for a backline that has sometimes been compelled to play Brayden Maynard on tall opponents.



Rory Sloane opined on Nine last week that Howe would be an ideal recruit for Essendon, as a veteran and educator of a young backline. One could argue the same of Richmond, who will lose Nathan Broad to West Coast or Gold Coast. View post on X Had Tasmania been entering the AFL a year earlier than 2028, Howe, as a Tassie man, would surely have been in their sights as a foundation leader who’d join their coaching panel after one or two years playing. Howe, slated to return for this Thursday night’s game in Adelaide, will have options, as will Pendlebury. For the latter, his stature as club and AFL legend is a significant incentive to remain a one-clubber. The Sherrin is in Collingwood’s court, as much as theirs. World.title: Shopkeeper survives leopard attack by a whisker
World.content:
WorldAsiaAnimal attacks Shopkeeper survives leopard attack by a whisker Lily Shanagher July 22, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A leopard lunged at men after bursting into a shop selling alcohol in India. Security camera footage of the store in Todaraisingh, Rajasthan, captured the animal leaping over the counter and pouncing on Sanjay Gurjar, 25. Loading The shopkeeper managed to shake off the leopard, which launched itself twice at him and grabbed his back, attempting to bite him, before he managed to run off, locking the animal inside. The big cat was then seen prowling around the empty shop, knocking over boxes before hiding under a shelf.



Related Article India Elusive big cats and humans live side by side in this alien-like landscape A second piece of footage taken in the storeroom shows the leopard lunging at a different man, Fateh Lal Koli, 40, knocking him across the room and to the floor before it dashes over the shelf and after Gurjar. Gurjar suffered claw injuries to his hand, shoulder and nose, while two other men also sustained injuries. The leopard had attacked a forest ranger volunteer on Sunday morning, officials told Indian media. The ranger had been investigating reports the leopard had been seen in bushes at 8.45am (Indian time) when the animal attacked him.



The animal then travelled into the northern town, where it entered the alcohol shop and attacked its second and third victims. A rescue team reached the town about 2pm and launched a five-hour operation to track and capture the leopard. Police cleared a cordon around the shop and shut the main market before calling in a specialist animal rescue unit. Officials said the leopard was a five-year-old male that will be given medical checks before being returned to the wild. Virender Singh Krishniya, deputy conservator of forests, said the animal was believed to have strayed into the town in search of prey after leaving surrounding forests. World.title: New York’s Mamdani says the city can’t arrest Netanyahu for war crimes
World.content:
WorldNorth AmericaTrump's America New York’s Mamdani says the city can’t arrest Netanyahu for war crimes Liam Stack July 22, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New York: Mayor Zohran Mamdani has challenged the federal government to execute an international arrest warrant against Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel, calling him a “war criminal” and “the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people” in a striking video statement. The mayor said the city’s law department explored whether the New York Police Department could arrest the Israeli prime minister during his expected visit to the city in September, but that the city did not have “independent legal authority” to do so. Loading The mayor’s announcement came days after he said in an interview with The New York Times Magazine that he had been in “active conversation” with the city’s law department about executing a warrant issued for Netanyahu in 2024 by the International Criminal Court. US President Donald Trump has ruled out any chance of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu being arrested. Getty Images



On Tuesday (US time), Mamdani said in the video that those conversations had led his administration to determine it does “not have the independent legal authority to enforce this warrant.” Related Article Analysis

US politics The kingmaker who stunned the US Democratic establishment – again Seated between the flags of the United States and New York City, Mamdani looked directly into the camera and solemnly told New Yorkers that Israel’s prime minister had no place visiting the city. “Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City, nor is any other war criminal at large,” Mamdani said. “While we cannot end the genocide on our own, we can decide whether our silence will become another weapon, and we can examine every tool we have to defend the humanity and dignity of all people.”



There appears to be no chance of federal law enforcement arresting Netanyahu in the near future. President Donald Trump said on Monday that the Israeli leader, whose country is a longtime US ally, would not be arrested in the United States “in any way, shape, or form”. The US is not a member of the International Criminal Court, which blunts the impact of the court’s warrant. On Tuesday night, Israel’s UN ambassador Danny Danon criticised Mamdani’s video in a statement posted online. “Enough with the blood libels,” Danon said. “You were elected to serve New Yorkers, not Hamas’ propaganda. Do your job!” Mayor Zohran Mamdani said he had been in “active conversation” with the New York City Law Department about executing a warrant issued for Netanyahu in 2024 by the International Criminal Court. AP Photo/Seth Wenig



Mamdani had said during his mayoral campaign that he would order the Police Department to arrest Netanyahu if he were to visit New York, as the prime minister is expected to do in September for the United Nations General Assembly. Related Article Israeli-Palestinian conflict The numbers that show what two years of war have done to Palestinian lives But the legal ability of the mayor to order such a move has long been in doubt. After he discussed the possibility with the Times last week, Mamdani was denounced by Netanyahu’s office, which said he “should focus on fixing the damage his policies have caused New York.” “Mamdani appears interested in diverting public attention from his follies and attacking the leader of the Jewish state and the only democracy in the Middle East,” the prime minister’s office said in a statement on Sunday. The mayor was also denounced on Monday by Danon, who said in an address to the General Assembly that there was “no legal basis” for Mamdani to order the arrest of Netanyahu. Danon accused him of engaging in “political theatre” to energise his “radical base.”



View post on X The international court issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his former defence minister, Yoav Gallant, in 2024 on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip, where more than 70,000 people have been killed in a war that began after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023, terrorist attack on Israel. The ICC warrants accused both Netanyahu and Gallant of having “intentionally and knowingly deprived” the population of Gaza of food, water, fuel and medicine, which both Netanyahu and Gallant have denied. The court also issued an arrest warrant for Hamas’ military chief, Muhammad Deif, for crimes against humanity, but Israel said it had killed Deif in an airstrike before the warrant could be issued. Israel’s conduct during the war in Gaza has been described as genocide by Israeli and international human rights groups, as well as by two separate UN commissions, one of which issued its findings last month.



Related Article Analysis

Middle East at war Trump claims he calls ‘all the shots’. Netanyahu and Iran have other ideas Israel has rejected those findings, and Netanyahu’s office said Sunday that “Israel has taken unprecedented wartime measures to minimise harm to civilians while confronting Hamas.” But Israel’s actions in Gaza have left it deeply isolated on the global stage and increasingly unpopular in the United States, its most important ally. According to the Pew Research Centre, polls show that a majority of Americans now hold a negative view of Israel, including majorities of adults under age 50 in both political parties. Among Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents, that number rises to 80 per cent.



This article originally appeared in The New York Times. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: As net closed in after 30 years, accused Chadstone shooter said he better ‘take the medicine’, court hears
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts As net closed in after 30 years, accused Chadstone shooter said he better ‘take the medicine’, court hears Erin Pearson July 22, 2026 — 3:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A great-grandfather and former rugby league player was allegedly tied to a violent Armaguard hold-up at Chadstone Shopping Centre after 30 years by DNA on a glove left at the scene by the gunman. As the net closed on Garry Sullivan, 78, he was captured on a listening device telling his wife it was time to “take the medicine”, a court has heard. Garry Sullivan during his extradition to Victoria. Nine News Sullivan was arrested in Queensland in May and extradited to Victoria after detectives reopened the 1994 case that left three people with gunshot wounds and $80,000 in cash missing. Melbourne Magistrates’ Court was told on Wednesday that Sullivan had escaped jail and was on the run when he allegedly used a pistol to hold up two Armaguard employees on May 16, 1994.



The court heard Sullivan allegedly shot one officer in the ankle, with the bullet ricocheting off him and through the right foot of a second guard. A third person, a bystander, was shot in the thigh as they attempted to follow the shooter to get his vehicle registration. The court heard that in the lead-up to the Chadstone incident, Sullivan and his stepfather had netted more than $3.2 million from robberies committed in the ’80s and ’90s, and were jailed for 20 years. The scene where two security guards were shot in May 1994 after being ambushed beside their Armaguard truck in a daylight heist that spilled into the busy Chadstone shopping centre. Nine News But Sullivan, the court heard, had cut a hole in a wire fence at the prison and escaped. During his time on the run he allegedly travelled to Chadstone. Sullivan was eventually rearrested in South Australia and locked up until 2005. He had been living in the community ever since, the prosecution said.



But court documents allege he was doing so with unexplained wealth. Sullivan is also charged with dealing in the proceeds of crime, about $366,000 police allege was laundered through his Tabcorp betting account between February 2020 and May 2026. Sullivan in his playing days. Of the money, $218,000 was withdrawn as Sullivan gambled prolifically while living in housing commission accommodation and on the pension. The court heard that when police reopened the Chadstone case, they compared a DNA sample of Sullivan that was on file with the glove from the scene, and it was “a billion to one” match. They then laid “bait” and captured him on listening devices correctly identifying to his wife the type of lead used to shoot the guards, the court was told.



“I’m just going to sit here and wait for them to come,” he allegedly told her. “I better take the medicine. You know what I mean.” Sverre Benjaminsen, one of two security guards shot on May 16, 1994. Nine News Sullivan applied to be freed on bail, which the prosecution opposed, comparing the man with ailing health to police killer Dezi Freeman, fearing he too could escape police apprehension once more. “It’s not that hard for somebody to abscond and if one has the means to do so, and there’s enough at stake,” prosecutor Francesca Holmes said.



Defence lawyer Matthew Cramer said his client was a father of four and grandfather of nine, a reformed family man who posed no risk of flight. His daughter, Kim Robertson, said her father had lived with his partner, Heather, for 49 years and had coeliac disease, pointing to a fall and 12-kilogram weight loss since his arrest. “He’s a regular granddad, he’s a regular dad to us,” she said. The court heard Sullivan had mouth cancer and heart disease, and his age added to his vulnerability in custody. Any alleged risk of flight was fanciful, Cramer said, with Sullivan having lived countless lives, including as a rugby league star, in the ’60s and ’70s, before his criminal notoriety began.



“We’re not Dezi Freeman,” Cramer said. “He’s now a dedicated family man.” Magistrate Patrick Southey agreed that Sullivan’s dedicated career as an armed robber in the ’80s and ’90 was “last millennium” and his fall from grace decades ago. He reminded those in the court of the presumption of innocence but maintained exceptional circumstances had not been established and refused bail. Sullivan is expected to return to court in October.
