World.title: Waikato hospitals revert to paperwork after major IT outage
World.content:
A massive IT outage is affecting hospitals across the Waikato region.

Health NZ spokesperson Stephanie Doe said a "network connectivity issue" had cut access to a number of applications used in Waikato hospitals.

This included Waikato, Thames, Te Kūiti, Tokoroa and Taumaranui.

"Where clinical systems are impacted, hospitals are reverting to manual processes to support continuity of care."

She said hospitals were prioritising urgent care and impacted patients would be contacted directly. Patients who have not been contacted should attend their appointments as normal.

She said the health agency was working to resolve the issue as quickly as possible.

But an email to staff said a timeline to resolve the issue was unknown.

It said theatres would continue for urgent and prioritised care.

Outpatient clinics have been postponed and the laboratory would be prioritising critical tests.

Radiology was to use a paper-based request system and could review images, but not send results.

World.title: Stuff's proposed job cuts come after tough years for local media industry
World.content:
Stuff Digital's latest proposed job cuts could see it lose editorial staff with deep institutional knowledge, but that was the "reality of media today", says a commentator.

The media company has confirmed that up to eight journalism jobs are on the line in a "simplified structure" of its editorial team.

The announcement of possible job losses at Stuff Digital are just the latest in a series of cuts across the local media sector over the past three years.

Gavin Ellis

Former NZ Herald editor-in-chief Gavin Ellis said cutting eight roles from a small digital team would be significant.

"You cannot take people out of an organisation as small as that, without it having an impact."

Stuff Digital said on Wednesday it had begun consultation with some of its editorial team on a simplified structure across national newsrooms which may result in a reduction of eight staff.

While there is a total Stuff Group editorial headcount of more than 300, that number mostly includes the masthead newspaper newsrooms. This proposal is believed to directly affect a team of about 30 to 40. The media firm said it was proposing to invest in new roles in its in-depth journalism team and in specialist content areas.

The E tū union said it was supporting members at Stuff Digital following the announcement.

Director Mat Danaher said having a properly resourced team of journalists and editors was "the best guarantee of accurate, distinctive and high-quality news".

"Technological change can support that work, but it should not be used to create a false sense of efficiency through staff cuts. Fewer journalists and editors inevitably means less capacity to cover stories, scrutinise those in power and produce the journalism New Zealanders rely on."

"E tū members understand that the media landscape is changing. They also believe New Zealand needs strong and sustainable news organisations, with enough professional journalists to produce the quality reporting our communities rely on. That requires media workers' skills, experience, and contribution to be properly recognised. Any proposed changes must be carefully considered, with genuine consultation and clear information provided to workers."

He said Stuff Digital was proposing to consolidate 19 journalist and reporter roles into 11 positions, reduce six editor roles to three, and remove four platform editor roles, a multimedia content producer role and the chief daily editor role.

Digital cuts a 'set-back'

Ellis said the latest cuts were a concern as the longer term strategy of media was a digital one.

"So cutting digital staff at this stage I think has got to be seen as a set back."

He said an advantage for Stuff was being able to use news content from mastheads - including The Post, The Press, and Sunday Star Times.

But Ellis said the company would be losing people with deep institutional knowledge.

"It's unfortunate, but it's the reality of media today."

Rival media firm NZME announced early last year that it was cutting almost 40 roles from the NZ Herald, BusinessDesk and Newstalk ZB news operation.

TVNZ cut about 68 jobs in 2024, while former rival Newshub shut down, resulting in 294 staff losing their jobs.

Whakaata Māori - formerly Māori Television - also cut 27 jobs at the end of 2024, while RNZ called for voluntary redundancies after its funding was cut in 2025.

"I live and hope that one day I'll start to see stories about media increasing their staff rather than decreasing," Ellis said.

The Spinoff founder Duncan Grieve said while the proposed cuts were very unpleasant, they were also part of running a newsroom at scale today.

"I feel deeply all of those affected, and yet at the same time, I can't bring myself to kind of cast blame on Stuff because this is something that's happening around newsrooms around the world all the time."

He felt that while people could judge where the cuts were focused, newsroom managers and executives typically had a good sense of where value lay in organisations.

Stuff Digital is co-owned by chief executive Sinead Boucher, while Trade Me bought 50 percent of the company last year.

The company split into two divisions - Stuff Digital and Masthead Publishing - in 2024.

World.title: Mum who suffered MRSA superbug warns against overusing antibiotics
World.content:
This story contains graphic details of medical conditions.

A global study has found New Zealand doctors are using too many antibiotics, risking the growth of superbugs.

An Invercargill mum who suffered for months with an antibiotic-resistant infection says something needs to change.

Jess Barnfather was infected with MRSA (Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) during a caesarean section at Dunedin Hospital in 2020.

NZ doctors using too many antibiotics, risking superbug growth Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

MRSA is a type of staph infection resistant to antibiotics like penicillin.

She said it took four weeks in hospital and six months at home to recover.

"It was probably the worst infection I've ever experienced in my lifetime," she said.

"So it first started off with my C-section incision having quite a lot of sharp stabbing pains every couple seconds... Once my wound had broken down, it opened up and all this pus had leaked out. I had a temperature so high, my face literally felt like it was on fire."

Because MRSA is resistant to typical treatments, Barnfather was given vancomycin, a much heavier antibiotic with a long list of side effects.

"That was pretty intense. Every time they would push it through my IV line, my vein would blow," she said.

"So my vein would basically collapse and it would literally burn my whole arm and my arm would swell every time."

Infectious disease doctor Steve Ritchie says as a country New Zealand is a high user of antibiotics. Supplied / Dr Steve Ritchie

Dr Steve Ritchie, an infectious disease doctor at Auckland City Hospital, said treating superbugs like MRSA was especially challenging.

"They're horrific. Infections caused by resistant bacteria create a whole range of problems, increase the cost of healthcare, the complexity of healthcare. They lead to longer lengths of hospital stay," he said.

"They're frankly a tragedy for the poor people who suffer them."

Global study finds doctors overuse antibiotics

The more antibiotics were used, the more opportunities bacteria had to grow resistant to them.

But a study published Wednesday in The Lancet medical journal found doctors around the world were using antibiotics more than they needed to.

Researchers estimated the ideal number of antibiotic doses, then compared those numbers with the real data.

In New Zealand, they suggested 14.3 daily doses for every 1000 people, but found the true figure was 24.1 doses.

Dr Ritchie said that sounded about right.

"They found an ideal rate for New Zealand and found that we are using antibiotics perhaps approaching two times that ideal rate, which is probably within the ballpark of reality," he said.

"It's fair to say we are high users of antibiotics."

Dr Prabani Wood says antibiotics are completely ineffective against viral infections although patients often asked for them for the flu or a cold. Supplied / Royal New Zealand College of GPs

Barnfather said her experience had made her keenly aware of how often antibiotics were prescribed.

"There is a complete overuse of antibiotics. Every time I take my kids to the doctor, here's some antibiotics," she said.

"Definitely there is a complete overuse of antibiotics and it's just ridiculous the amount that's given."

Dr Prabani Wood, the medical director for the Royal College of GPs, said patients often asked for antibiotics to treat a cold or flu.

But in reality she said they were completely ineffective against viral infections.

"[They] feel sick, can't go to work, they've got a cough... I think there is still that public perception amongst big groups of the population that antibiotics are the answer," she said.

"But often it's a case of rest, taking fluids and simple pain relief."

Dr Ritchie said work was being done across the sector to reduce the use of antibiotics.

"In veterinary care and agriculture, the use of antibiotics has dropped considerably," he said.

"People in New Zealand have developed a national antibiotic guideline, [and] in our hospitals, we have a small group of really dedicated pharmacists and doctors looking at antibiotic use and trying to optimise antibiotic use."

World.title: Law Commission urges stronger hate crime laws, not new offences
World.content:
Hate crime laws are not working well in practice, but the existing legal framework should be improved rather than creating new offences, the Law Commission has found.

In its report set to be tabled in Parliament on Wednesday, the commission found the current approach of giving longer sentences for crimes motivated by hate remained the most appropriate model.

Hate speech, and making behaviour that was not already considered an offence illegal, were out of scope of the review.

"While we do consider whether to create new hate crime offences, they would only apply to acts (such as assault) that are already an offence ... our focus is on how the justice system should respond when offending is found to have been motivated by hostility towards a group of people."

The commission said it did not recommend creating new hate crime offences because it was "unlikely that hate crime offenders would be consistently charged with or convicted of" them.

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Such offences would be more difficult to prove, making the law more complex and in some cases could mean hate offending was not tackled at all.

However, the current regime also faced problems, including that courts did not need to state publicly when a crime was motivated by hate, such crimes were not well documented, and the law did not ensure courts knew prosecutors and police though a crime was motivated by hate or hostility.

The report made 12 recommendations*:

Change charging documents to say when hostility or prejudice (hate) should be considered an aggravating factor (under section 9(1)(h) of the Sentencing Act) by amending the Sentencing and Criminal Procudure Acts. Courts would be able to add or remove this at any time, but must permanently record when the section is used at sentencing.

Have courts share with police and Corrections when charging documents include that hate crime section, and include that detail on permanent court records.

Include details about the people, groups or characteristics targeted when the court shares this information, where technically feasible.

When someone is convicted of a crime motivated by hate towards a group of people with a specific characteristic, require courts to say so

Remove the requirement for the offender to believe the victim had the relevant characteristic by repealing Section 9(1)(h)(ii) of the Sentencing Act

Add 'sex' to the list of example characteristics, to make clear that targeting someone based on their sex - particularly women - should be considered a hate crime

Have police review and update guidance, to ensure officers and prosecutors know of law changes from this review

Have police share that updated guidance with Crown solicitors

Have police and Crown Solicitors provide training on the law changes, supported by Crown Law

Give judges training and guidance on the law changes, through the Institute of Judicial Studies

Police should publish annual data on hate crimes

Ministry of Justice should publish annual court data on hate crime cases

* Wording has been changed for clarity and brevity

The commission said it did not recommend using the terms "hate" or "hate crime" in legislation, instead focusing on hostility to groups of people, but noted the terms were common and the report used them as they were shorter and easier to understand than alternatives.

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said the goverment's primary focus was on reducing the number of victims of crime.

"The report shows that in a broad sense our current hate crime laws are working. Rather than recommending we create a bespoke offence, the commission has identified areas it believes could be improved," he said.

"We will consider their recommendations in due course."

The review was launched by the Law Commission in early 2024 after the coalition ordered a halt to a separate review of hate speech.

The previous Labour government had planned to bring in hate speech laws in response to the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Christchurch terrorist attacks, which recommended ensuring hate speech and hate crime laws were fit for purpose.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

This included the creation of specific hate-motivated offences under the Summary Offences Act and the Crimes Act.

However, Labour faced significant public backlash over its hate speech changes by free speech proponents after failing to clearly explain what would be classed as hate speech.

Labour later withdrew its proposed legislation and referred the matter to the Law Commission, but the coalition scrapped that review in favour of this one.

The commission noted that although hate speech was outside its scope, "a significant number of individuals and groups raised the issue during consultation".

Destiny Church leader Brian Tamaki. RNZ / Angus Dreaver

Concern about hate speech resurfaced in recent weeks after Destiny Church leader Brian Tamaki called on followers to "purge" Hindus, Sikhs and Muslims including by burning down mosques and temples.

Political parties had mixed stances, with the Greens and Te Pāti Māori saying they supported legislating against hate speech, National saying it did not, ACT calling for more enforcement of current laws, and Labour promising to share a detailed policy in due course.

NZ First did not respond at the time.

World.title: Union says north Waikato prison staff shortcutting putting 'public at risk'
World.content:
The union representing prison staff says staff shortcutting at a north Waikato prison is only putting the public at more risk.

Short-staffing, low staff morale, no onsite drug testing for years, contraband readily available, and filthy uninhabitable parts of the jail were just some of the serious concerns identified at the Spring Hill Correctional Facility.

A report by the inspectorate office also highlights issues with staff absences and inexperience, long lockdowns for inmates, inadequate meals, clothing and bedding.

The prison was over capacity for its original design as an end destination site for 650 prisoners. It had essentially became a remand site, Chief Inspector Janis Adair said, housing over 800 prisoners at the time of inspection. The report found this change in population proving a challenge for the site's infrastructure and staff alike.

The inspection found custodial staffing levels were at 94 percent, but that morale was low amongst custodial staff and unplanned absences, like sick leave, were common and left units short staffed.

"The lack of availability of custodial staff and the unsuitable infrastructure had significant impacts across the prison."

Corrections Association New Zealand president Floyd du Plessis said the report was not surprising.

"The component that is surprising to us is the statement from Corrections that these things have all been addressed and progressed. From what our members are saying on the floor, the people that work in that prison on the floor every day, they haven't seen an improvement. They're still seeing daily occurrences of short staffing. Corners being cut and safety still a continual issue."

He said overall staffing numbers had increased, but due to financial restraints were still not covering shifts.

"Where staff are sick or short, they're not putting on additional shifts to replace those and so on a daily basis, they're actually still running short just for a different reason.

"The fact that prisoners aren't able to be brought out for programs, interviews, health checks, and that drives that tension and concern, and that's exactly the problem the report identified, but we're still seeing that same problem occurring now."

He said when a prison isn't staffed properly it just means rehabilitation programmes and interventions weren't able to happen, so prisoners were sitting there with no reintegration or offending needs addressed.

Then, they're being released, having not gone through all of those programmes to improve.

"That puts the community at an even greater risk than they already are," du Plessis said.

"We can't shortcut staffing in a place like a prison. The staffing's built to the minimum we possibly need to safely run and as soon as you do any reduction in that, things stop. And the first thing that stops is those programs, those interventions, those interviews that are needed to help identify chronogenic needs and all those interventions that are required to help change their way of thinking.

"A prison that's running badly puts the public at risk. It's not some hidden thing that sits in a corner.

"Unfortunately, it all comes down to fiscal. They see it as a financial line item, we see it as a safety thing... As much as people think it's forgotten, all of these people get released, all of them come back to the community. Unless we improve it, public and staff have been placed at risk."

He said staff felt extremely at risk.

"We have regular reports from staff that they're not feeling safe. They're cutting corners to just get through the day. Every time they cut a corner, they're putting themselves at risk and they're facing a lot of backlash.

"So when prisoners don't get out, when they don't get access to those different programs or nurses and the like. They lash out, they get frustrated, and they lash out at staff, and we're seeing that on a weekly basis."

That, he said ranges anywhere from ongoing threats of violence to actual violence on a daily basis.

"The more staff you have, the more you can do and that's the key. We keep trying to get more done with less stuff. And in an environment like ours with the risks and concerns we face, it's just impossible. It's either safety or it's not. And the reality is you can't do anything more unless you make it safe and the only way to make it safer is more staff.

"Nintety-nine per cent of corrections officers join the job because they want to make a difference. They want to work and get these things running right. But it's hard when you're short staff and you're just not able to."

Corrections custodial services commissioner Sean Mason said, in response to the report, it was positive to see many of the areas identified for improvement in the report aligned with work Corrections had already addressed or that was underway since the inspection was carried out more than a year ago.

"Many prisoners go to extreme lengths to get contraband into prisons and Corrections is constantly working to stay one step ahead in contraband prevention."

Drug testing was reintroduced in November 2025 after it was suspended during the Covid-19 pandemic, he said, when all non-essential prison activities were paused to reduce operational risks and support public health requirements and when staffing pressures were at their tightest.

Mason also said following an extensive nationwide recruitment drive, there was now an additional 45 custodial staff working at the site, and this had reduced the day-to-day impact on the prison when staff called in sick.

World.title: Call to make it mandatory for some businesses to report their gender pay gap
World.content:
A group of high profile pay equity campaigners are calling for politicians to do more to close the pay equity gap.

Global Women is calling for cross party support to make it mandatory for businesses of a certain size to report their gender pay gap.

At the moment it is voluntary for businesses to report their pay gaps.

But Global Women said full disclosure will support greater transparency, fairer workplaces and a more productive economy, and on Wednesday they published an open letter making their case.

According to the Ministry for Women, the pay gap for New Zealand women across the board is 5.2 percent.

STILLMindingTheGap.nz has also been campaigning for urgent action to reduce New Zealand's gender and ethnic pay gaps.

Calls for cross party support on mandatory pay gap reporting Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

Campaign manager Jo Cribb told Checkpoint the gender pay gap had a massive impact on a women's earnings over her career.

"It's costing a woman who sort of earns the median wage over her career about $250,000."

She said it was government's inaction that was contributing to that cost, by not putting mandatory reporting in place.

If introduced, she said a mandatory reporting system would drop the pay gap.

"If the government introduced compulsory reporting, it would drop New Zealand's pay gaps by about 20 to 40 percent.

"If you think about that over a week, a woman earning the median wage would earn about $33.76 more."

Cribb said if businesses could not justify a reason for a pay gap within their company, then that money was owed.

"It's illegal, but surely they'd want to fix that, and we know that many, many businesses do."

She said research by Berl, commissioned by STILLMindingTheGap.nz had found that around 50 percent of organisations which looked at their pay gaps did increase the wages of women because they found they could not justify the gaps.

The gender pay gap was 5.2 percent in 2025 but was much worse for some ethnic groups - 12 percent for wāhine Māori, almost 16 percent for Pacific women and about 10 percent for Asian women.

Cribb said further research had also found that if factors like a woman's education level, work experience, the industry she worked in or how many hours she worked were accounted for, than 80 percent of gender pay gaps could not be explained.

"It's got nothing to do with individuals, we can attribute that, then the gender pay gap in New Zealand is directly related to the decisions that managers make in organisations about how much people are paid.

"So this is actually all about what happens within businesses."

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon recently said he believed publicly reporting pay gap data was the right thing to do, and that making it compulsory for businesses was worth a conversation.

The National leader has not committed to a campaign policy on the matter, but said other policies indicated the party's direction on pay parity.

The coalition government halted all pay equity claims last year and made it harder to lodge new ones, a move that was heavily criticised by advocates.

Cribb said the government should not be worrying about the compliance cost associated with pay gap reporting.

"The large piece of research that we did showed that it costs most businesses less than 10 hours of staff time a year... so there's very little compliance cost."

She said the benefits to the economy could be up to $18 billion.

"If we have the workforce working more efficiently if we've got the talent being promoted. We also find the business benefits are around people are more productive, they're more engaged, they come to work happier because they're being treated fairly.

"If women are paid more, they pay more tax and they also, their families take less working for families and other benefits."

World.title: Opponents of plan to bulldoze Canterbury golf course rally outside Parliament
World.content:
Opponents of a controversial plan to bulldoze Canterbury's Pegasus Golf Course to make way for hundreds of homes have rallied outside Parliament.

Developer Wolfbrook bought the 18-hole, 77-hectare golf course in May and plans to redevelop the land into housing using the government's fast-track consent process.

The proposal has been met by widespread opposition from locals, Waimakariri mayor Dan Gordon, Waimakariri MP Matt Doocey and Labour's North Canterbury-based list MP Dan Rosewarne.

Pegasus Residents' Group spokesperson Matt James said more than 16,000 people signed the petition presented to Parliament on Wednesday.

It called for the project not to by-pass the usual consenting process.

"Fast-track legislation has its place. It's there to facilitate the relatively quick development of key critical infrastructure that New Zealand needs. It was never there to be a back-door planning process for residential developers and that's increasingly what's happening," James said.

"Pegasus has roughly 4000 residents but we had over 16,000 people sign our petition because people quickly saw it as an issue far bigger than Pegasus."

Matt James says the petition calls for the development project not to by-pass the usual consenting process. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

James said the fast-track process gave those affected less opportunity to have a say.

"The Waimakariri District Council have done their planning for the future, they did that only last year, they've identified the areas of growth in the district and Pegasus was never on that plan. It doesn't need to be on that plan," he said.

Locals were continuing to work with the Waimakariri District Council to buy the golf course off Wolfbrook, James said.

A fundraising golf tournament held at Amberley Golf Club last weekend had raised about $3000 for the campaign, he said.

"We're eager to defend our cause. The petition will lead to us being invited to attend a select committee hearing at some stage. Obviously the key thing is the assumption that Wolfbrook will make their proposal officially very shortly and that will start the clock ticking for Minister [Chris] Bishop to give a response. We will be waiting with bated breath on that."

Dan Gordon has said that the move was disappointing for those who wanted to see the golf course, which was a community asset, protected. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Earlier this month James said Wolfbrook had further inflamed tensions by blocking paths and filling holes with concrete at the golf course.

People were dismayed to discover the "unnecessary and childish" concreted holes after communication broke down between the developer and the wider community, James said.

From left Matt James, Labour's North Canterbury-based list MP Dan Rosewarne and Waimakariri MP Matt Doocey. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

In June Waimakariri mayor Dan Gordon said Wolfbrook had notified the council it intended to use the fast-track consenting process to rezone the land for housing.

"This is disappointing news for the thousands of residents and supporters who want to see this important community asset protected," he said, at the time.

"Council's view is clear - developments that sit outside established growth areas, identified in our recently consulted on and adopted district plan and which have previously been considered and rejected through district planning or other Resource Management Act processes, should not be eligible for the fast-track pathway. However, any decision on an application will ultimately rest with the ministers."

World.title: West Papua rebels claim responsibility for killing three indigenous Papuan 'traitors'
World.content:
West Papuan militants have claimed responsibility for the deaths of three indigenous Papuans, who they claim were supplying intelligence to Indonesia.

In a statement, the West Papua National Liberation Army (TPNPB) said the three were executed in Yahukimo as traitors to Papua's independence movement.

It claims to have evidence that the three Papuans had caused the deaths of several TPNPB troops.

Along with the three Papuans, the TPNPB also killed an Indonesian Brimob police officer.

The TPNPB said the executions were a warning to all Papuans not to engage with the Indonesian military, and that they will execute anybody that does.

The TPNPB executed an American pilot, Nicholas Gosselin, after he flew a small aircraft into Yahukimo earlier this month.

A spokesperson for the TPNPB said foreigners had been warned not to fly into the area, which the Army considers an active war zone.

Allegations by the TPNPB that the company Gosselin flew for PT AMA had been helping transport Indonesian military, has been rejected by the company and the government.

World.title: Lewis breaks Australian 100m record, beats five-time Olympic champ
World.content:
Torrie Lewis has set a new Australian women's 100 metres record after breaking her own national record at a meet in Slovakia.

Lewis ran a time of 11.04 seconds, beating her previous record time of 11.08 as she beat out Jamaica's five-time Olympic champion Elaine Thompson-Herah, who finished in second.

The 21-year-old Lewis also competed in and won the 200m event, where she ran a 22.66.

It is the third separate time Lewis has broken the Australian 100m record, having previously done so as a 19-year-old in 2024 by running an 11.10 before lowering that mark to 11.08 at last year's World Championships.

Lewis beat out Jamaican sprint icon Elaine-Thompson Herah (pictured). (Getty: Al Bello)

Lewis made her Olympic debut in the 200m event in Paris two years ago and finished in the semifinals after running a then-personal-best time of 22.89. She also competed in the 4x100m event in Paris.

The women's 100m record is owned by late American sprint legend Florence Griffith-Joyner, who ran a 10.49 at the US Olympic trials in 1988. Thompson-Herah holds the second-fastest 100m mark of all time at 10.54.

Griffith-Joyner also holds the world record for the 200m, 21.34, a mark she set at the 1988 Olympics in Seoul.

Both records are among the longest-standing across all women's athletics.

The career-best 100m time comes at the perfect time for Lewis, who is poised to compete in the 100m, 200m and 4x100m relay events at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

World.title: Fox sisters combine in 'dream team' for gold medals at World Championships
World.content:
The gold rush at the world titles has continued for Jess Fox, with the canoe slalom legend spearheading the Australian women's kayak team to victory in Oklahoma.

A day after three-time Olympic champion Fox claimed gold in the kayak cross time trial event, the 32-year-old joined her younger sister Noemie Fox and Kate Eckhardt at the top of the podium.

The victory at Riversport Rapids on Tuesday (Wednesday AEST) continued Fox's successful return to competition since undergoing surgery to remove a tumour from a kidney last August.

Loading Instagram content

It is the second title for the trio after winning gold in London in 2023 in the same event, which is only contested at the world championships.

Competing on the same course that will host the canoe slalom at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, the Australians used experience and expertise in their clinical run to put pressure on the final three teams.

In third place heading into the final third of the race, the trio lifted to complete a clean run through the gates and finish 0.64 seconds ahead of France and Slovakia.

"We're a bit of a dream team," Noemie said.

"We've been training so well and supporting each other. There was so much trust and support in the lead in, and we felt so good and wanted to do our best out there.

"To share these moments and be so proud of what we've done and to have those moments in an individual sport where we can collectively push each other and celebrate together is so special.

"It was just so much fun out there and to be rewarded with a gold medal is amazing, and I'm so proud of our double title now."

The golden girls also had success in the individual kayak race, with all qualifying for the top 30 semifinals.

Despite posting the fastest time of the day, Jess Fox, who is chasing a 16th world title, was docked for two gate touches and progressed in ninth place.

Jess Fox is chasing a 16th world title. (ABC News: Sean Tarek Goodwin)

"A bit of a shaky start with the two touches back-to-back, but overall it was then solid and I kept the boat speed on and I knew I would have to push to qualify because you never know — that top 30 can be really tight especially on a course like this," she said.

Eckhardt qualified in 11th position and Noemie was 25th.

In the men's kayak teams final, the Australian men had an unfortunate 50-second penalty in their run and finished 18th.

They had better luck in the individual kayak heats, with all six paddlers progressing through to the K1 semi-finals.

Olympian Tim Anderson was the best of the Aussies in eighth.

AAP

World.title: Former Socceroos captain Paul Wade reveals probable CTE diagnosis
World.content:
Former Socceroos captain Paul Wade has revealed he has been diagnosed with "probable" chronic traumatic encephalopathy, which has been linked to repeated head knocks and injuries.

In a statement put out by Professional Footballers Australia (PFA) on Wednesday, Wade said he was diagnosed in late 2024 with a suspected case of the disease after experiencing neurological symptoms.

He said this was upgraded after further assessments to probable in 2025.

The disease can only be confirmed after death.

"They did the tests … and [the neurologists] went, 'Oh, we've got a real problem here'," he told the ABC.

Symptoms of the disease can include depression, memory loss, tremors, poor impulse control and suicidal thoughts.

After scans showed it was probable CTE he said he just "stood there" and thought "am I going to die from this?"

Wade revealed a diagnosis of probable chronic traumatic encephalopathy. (7.30)

Wade's neurologist Rowena Mobbs made the "probable" diagnosis after two years of monitoring his symptoms and extensive testing.

Dr Mobbs said neurologists across Australia started using "probable" diagnoses to refer patients to the right treatment.

"It's not about fear, it's not about giving any definitive diagnosis, but it's about getting appropriate care and support to people," she said.

"I think Paul and his family want to see people in the community feeling confident that they can come forward for help and getting that right dementia care."

'He knew something was wrong'

Wade, who now lives on the Central Coast, north of Sydney, said receiving the diagnosis was "difficult" but wanted to share his experience to raise awareness of concussion and brain health across all levels of football.

"Football gave me so much. It gave me a life, a career, incredible experiences and the privilege of representing Australia," he said.

" But I also must be honest about the challenges I now face and the uncertainty that comes with living with a neurodegenerative condition. "

Asked whether the probable diagnosis was linked to his time playing, he said "it must have had something to do with it".

"I think about the number of times at a training session I headed a ball."

Dr Mobbs said Wade expressed a level of "validation" when he received the "probable" diagnosis.

"He knew it in himself… He knew something was wrong, he knew it felt different," she said.

Doctor urges ban to headers by children

Rowena Mobbs said Wade's diagnosis came after "extensive testing". (ABC News: Michael Nudl)

After 30 years of exposure to head knocks in soccer, including headers, Dr Mobbs said repetitive traumatic brain injury was the "main burden" for Wade.

Dr Mobbs urged Football Australia to ban headers for children playing soccer under the age of 12.

"We must hold onto our activity and sport in life, for our kids especially, but we need to lower the repetitive head injury burden," she said.

"That's where we need good care in the community, with our excellent health systems, the government to step in and provide funding for research, and for us all to be aware of our lifetime burden of head injury and try and prevent it where possible."

Sixty-four-year-old Wade, who led the national team for six years in the 1990s, said more understanding was needed about the long-term effects of repeated head impacts to "protect future generations".

"If sharing my experience can help someone seek support, create better education and prevention, or help the game take brain health more seriously, then it is worth doing," Wade, who also lives with epilepsy, said.

'Advancement of the game'

Wade's announcement comes less than a month after Four Corner's revealed 33 Australian Rules players had been diagnosed with CTE.

Wade (left) leading out the Socceroos for the 1993 Australia v Argentina FIFA World Cup play-off match. (Getty Images: Joe Mann/Offside)

He said people concerned should not stop playing contact sports "because if you do we're going to have an even bigger problem with mental health and wellbeing".

"To the people actually making the rules we've got to come up with ways we can make it safer," Wade said.

"If I could say to Football Australia, or even FIFA, if you're listening, let's put some protocols in there because you've got everything about concussion.

"[But] you don't talk about CTE and how we can change the game and change the training and change the age so that it's minimalised, so we're not exposing kids to CTE."

He asked who was going to "stand up and be brave and say no", and assert boundaries.

"Someone's got to say no. Kids are … heading a ball 12 years or under. Make it 14, I don't care," he said.

PFA chief executive Beau Busch said Wade's decision to open up about his diagnosis was an "important act of leadership".

"In sharing his story Paul has once again illustrated his truly remarkable commitment to the advancement of the game," Mr Busch said.

"He is doing so not only for himself but for the players and families who are facing, or may one day face, similar questions about brain health."

Mr Busch said Australian football must be proactive in tackling brain injuries "through better policies, research, education and support for former players".

A decorated career

Wade, who was born in England in 1962, came to Australia at 11 years of age with a passion for football, moving his way up to senior positions within Victorian clubs including Croydon, Green Gully, Brunswick and South Melbourne.

In 1985 he claimed a spot in the Australian team, playing his first full international against Czechoslovakia the following year.

He then captained the Australian soccer side from 1990 to 1996.

Wade was captain of the Socceroos for six years. (News Video)

On Football Australia's website Wade is credited with 345 national league appearances, 119 matches played for Australia, and 84 full internationals.

Wade also played in the 1988 Olympic Games and two World Cup qualifying campaigns.

After he retired as a player he became involved with TV commentary and coaching clinics for kids.

His career and the impacts of his neurodegenerative condition will be explored in an upcoming mini documentary being produced by PFA.

World.title: Spanish chief accuses FIFA boss of 'destroying the football industry'
World.content:
Gianni Infantino should resign as head of FIFA for "destroying the football industry" by expanding international competitions, according to Javier Tebas, the president of Spain's football league La Liga

It is not the first time he has lashed out at Infantino over fixture congestion and for considering a proposal to expand the 2030 men's World Cup from 48 teams to 64.

"Increasing the number of national teams makes no sense. The football industry isn't just the World Cup, which is the most important event. But not everything can revolve around the World Cup," Tebas told La Gazzetta dello Sport.

Players and fans made the World Cup a success, but the politics shouldn't be forgotten The biggest ever World Cup brought diverse communities together and galvanised its non-traditional footballing co-hosts, but the concerns raised from the start have not disappeared in the positive afterglow.

"In my opinion, yes, I think his time is up," he said of Infantino. "However, he has the support of the system and the federations, so there's not much more to add, is there? There's no opposition candidate, nobody wants to stand just to lose. This is the system and it's rotten at its core.

"He shouldn't stay, but he won't leave. I've heard many people who are against Infantino. They say it, but then they do nothing. I don't know what's worse, the silence or the complicity, because those who stay silent are perfectly aware of the damage football is suffering."

South American soccer's ruling body CONMEBOL has made an official proposal to expand the 2030 World Cup to 64 teams. The competition is already set to be the most sprawling edition, with six host nations spread across three continents.

"It's national competition that sustains this sport," Tebas added. "They are destroying the football industry, which generates tens of thousands of jobs, for an event that lasts 40 days and involves a minority of players."

The World Cup final had a 27-minute half-time interval thanks to a half-time show featuring artists such as Justin Bieber (pictured). (Reuters: Amanda Perobelli)

He also criticised world football's governing body FIFA over the new hydration breaks implemented at the World Cup, which ended on Sunday, as well as the extended 27-minute half-time interval — rather than the standard 15 — during the final, in which Spain defeated Argentina 1-0.

The hydration breaks midway through each half were introduced to help players deal with the summer heat in the United States, Canada and Mexico. But critics say they had unintended consequences, ruining the flow of the game and giving coaches a chance to tactically shift momentum in their team's favour.

"FIFA arranges things as it pleases, for what it wants, for its own interests, certainly not for football," Tebas said. "Hydration breaks are a lie. We have them in La Liga, but only when it's genuinely hot. Here, the pitches in Dallas, Los Angeles, and Atlanta had air conditioning. It was a lie and just a break for advertising."

Infantino announced in April that he would run for re-election for a fourth term as president. The vote for the 2027–2031 period is scheduled for March 18 in Morocco.

La Liga boss Javier Tebas has not been shy about attacking Infantino in the past. (Getty Images: Oscar J. Barroso/Europa Press)

The Football Supporters Europe (FSE) group also called on the wider soccer community to hold FIFA to account.

In a statement on its website headlined "A World Cup that failed supporters", the FSE demanded "structural governance reforms to hand decision-making power back to the FIFA Council and Congress and ensure full consultation with clubs, leagues, players and supporters".

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

It added: "The 2026 World Cup should have been a celebration of the game and the supporters who give it life. Instead, it has too often become a case study in what is so deeply wrong with football today.

"From the outset, supporters were asked to place their trust in FIFA and "chill", but it prioritised spectacle and commercialisation over the match-going experience with key elements of football's identity being messed with. Over the last month, we've seen football contorted to the whim of Gianni Infantino and the Trump administration."

The FSE, accepted by European soccer's governing body UEFA as the recognised group representing fans in the region, then went on to attack "historically high ticket prices" and "skyrocketing transportation costs, bending of rules and procedures, exclusion of swathes of the global population and a lack of transparent communication".

"All this created an environment of confusion and distrust that has severely damaged the reputation of FIFA, the World Cup, and the integrity of football itself," its statement said.

"The lessons from this World Cup are clear: FIFA is unfit to govern global football. The future of the game cannot rest in the hands of a man who has proven yet again that he puts financial and political interests ahead of the future of our game."

AP

World.title: Cameron McEvoy has lived a life between trips to Glasgow
World.content:
When Cameron McEvoy travelled to Glasgow in 2014, he was a 19-year-old "kid".

Twelve years later, he returns to the site of his Commonwealth Games debut as a completely different man with a completely different outlook on a sport that is almost unrecognisable.

McEvoy emerged as part of the ill-fated batch of sprint stars at the 2012 Olympics — the so-called "weapons of mass destruction" who returned from London without a gold medal from any male swimmer.

Two years later, McEvoy won six medals, including two relay golds, at the Commonwealth Games despite still trying to find his place in the squad.

"I still felt like a new person on the team back in 2014," he told reporters at Glasgow airport on Wednesday morning (AEST).

Cam McEvoy says his 50m freestyle world record is just the beginning When Cameron McEvoy broke the long-standing 50m freestyle world record in March, he was at great pains to note that he believes he can go even faster.

"I was super shy; I wasn't really outspoken. I'm in the same sport but the way I'm conducting training on a day-to-day basis, the way being on the team feels now compared to as a rookie, almost feels like it's a new sport.

"It's going to be almost nostalgic being back at the Tollcross pool, seeing the set-up and going through the same thing I did as a teenager."

As he and the Dolphins touched down in the Scottish capital once again, McEvoy is a brand new man and one of only two Australian swimmers, along with Lakeisha Patterson, back for another go.

"A lot has changed," he said.

"I was basically a kid [in 2014], and now I've got my own kid. Things are very different now.

A baby-faced McEvoy won three individual silvers as part of a six-medal haul in Glasgow 12 years ago. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

"There's actually a member on the swim team who's 14 [Mia Hogan], so she was only two when I was back here competing last time.

"A lot has happened; basically, my entire international career has unfolded."

Do you know an athlete competing at the Commonwealth Games? Share with us Whether you are you a family member, a friend, a colleague or a coach, share your connection with us and how you will be supporting them.

McEvoy missed out on individual medals at his first three Olympic Games and is surprisingly still hunting his first individual Commonwealth gold.

At Glasgow 2014 he finished second in the 50m, 100m and 200m. At his home Games on the Gold Coast in 2018, the pain was amplified when he picked up bronze in the 50m but missed the medals in the 100m despite entering as the Commonwealth record holder and fastest qualifier for the final.

McEvoy struggled to bounce back from those setbacks, particularly at Rio 2016 and Gold Coast 2018, to the point that when the last Commonwealth Games were on, he was at home considering his future in the sport.

He said he was "in the wilderness", unsure if he wanted to continue swimming after so many painful disappointments, but teammate Elijah Winnington's mental resilience got him back in the pool.

"Elijah had just won the 400m freestyle world title on the back of falling short in Tokyo [2021 Olympics]. For me, I saw that as a massive inspiration," he said.

"I fell short in Rio and couldn't bounce back that following year, but seeing Elijah go from Tokyo seventh in the 400m final to world champion, that was definitely a factor in motivating me to want to take that next step and come back."

ABC Sport will be live blogging every day of the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.
